channel.title: SQE Daily
channel.description: One free SQE1 practice question every day, with a worked answer and the legal source.

item.title: Taking will instructions from a relative: acting only on the client's own instructions (SRA Code para 3.1)
item.description:
Ravi Mehta telephones Elm Street Solicitors and asks Laura Bennett, a solicitor, to prepare a new will for his mother, Kamala, aged 88. Ravi says Kamala wants to leave her whole estate to him instead of dividing it equally between him and his sister, as her existing will does. Ravi will bring Kamala in to sign, pay the firm's fees and has emailed a typed list of 'Mum's wishes'. Laura has never spoken to Kamala, and Ravi says Kamala is too tired to come to the phone.
Which of the following best describes how Laura should proceed under the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors?

item.title: Hybrid public authorities and private acts under the Human Rights Act 1998 s.6(3)(b) and (5)
item.description:
Ferrous Secure Services Ltd is a private company. Under a contract with the Home Office it runs an immigration detention centre, holding people detained under statutory immigration powers. It also has ordinary commercial contracts, including its contract of employment with Lena Novak, an office cleaner at its head office. In 2026 Rashid, a detainee, alleges that the conditions in which the company holds him breach his Convention rights. Separately, Lena is dismissed and argues that the company is bound by s.6 of the Human Rights Act 1998 in relation to her dismissal.
Which of the following best describes the application of s.6 of the Human Rights Act 1998 to the company?

item.title: Which activities are reserved legal activities? Probate activities v will-writing (Legal Services Act 2007 s.12 and Sch 2)
item.description:
Kwame Asante runs Cornerstone Estate Services, a small business that is not authorised by the SRA or any other approved regulator, and none of its staff is an authorised person. He plans to expand and lists the services he would like to offer clients for a fee from 2026: drafting wills, advising on inheritance tax planning, acting as a mediator in family disputes about estates, preparing the papers needed to apply for grants of probate, and writing letters to banks on behalf of executors asking for account balances.
Which of the following best identifies the service that is a reserved legal activity under the Legal Services Act 2007?

item.title: Recoverable damage under the Consumer Protection Act 1987: the product itself is excluded (s.5)
item.description:
Megan Doyle bought a dehumidifier for £180 to use in her flat. In June 2026 a defect in its wiring caused it to catch fire while she was at home. The dehumidifier was completely destroyed, the fire damaged Megan's sofa, which will cost £900 to replace, and Megan suffered burns to her hand while putting the fire out. She brings a claim against the manufacturer under Part I of the Consumer Protection Act 1987, and it is accepted that the product was defective.
Which of the following best describes the damage Megan can recover under Part I of the Act?

item.title: Damages for negligent misrepresentation and the reverse burden of proof (Misrepresentation Act 1967 s.2(1))
item.description:
In January 2026 Tom Ellery agreed to buy a café business from Sunita Rao for £120,000. During negotiations Sunita told Tom that the café's annual turnover was £400,000. She took the figure from accounts that were three years old and did not check the current figures, although they were readily available to her. Relying on the figure, Tom signed the contract. The real current turnover was about £250,000, and Tom has suffered loss as a result. Sunita did not know the figure was wrong and did not intend to deceive Tom. The statement was not made a term of the contract.
Which of the following best describes Tom's position if he claims damages under the Misrepresentation Act 1967?

item.title: Summary judgment: no real prospect and no other compelling reason for a trial (CPR 24.3 and 24.4)
item.description:
Brennan Tiles Ltd supplied £62,000 of tiles to Marlow Fit-Out Ltd, which has not paid. Brennan issued a claim in the County Court and Marlow filed an acknowledgment of service, but has not yet filed a defence. Marlow's only stated reason for not paying is that its own customer has not paid it. The contract between Brennan and Marlow makes no reference to Marlow's customer, and Marlow accepts that the tiles were delivered and were of satisfactory quality. Brennan wants to end the claim quickly without a trial.
Which of the following best describes whether Brennan can obtain summary judgment?

item.title: Changing the nature of a partnership business needs every partner's consent (Partnership Act 1890 s.24(8))
item.description:
Amara, Ben, Chloe and Dev have run a vegan catering business together as a general partnership since 2022. They have no written partnership agreement and have never agreed anything about how decisions are made. In March 2026 Amara, Ben and Chloe vote to close the catering side and turn the firm into a wedding and events venue business, using the partnership's kitchen premises as a function hall. Dev objects strongly and refuses to agree. The other three say that, as a clear majority, they are entitled to go ahead.
Which of the following best describes the legal position on the proposed change?

item.title: Extending detention without charge from 24 to 36 hours (PACE 1984 ss.41 and 42)
item.description:
Hannah Brooks was arrested at her home at 08:15 on Monday 9 November 2026 on suspicion of fraud by false representation, an either-way offence. She arrived at the police station at 09:00 that day. Her detention has been reviewed twice. At 07:30 on Tuesday, officers still need to interview her about documents seized from her office. The investigation is being conducted diligently and expeditiously, and further detention is necessary to obtain evidence by questioning her. Her solicitor, Imran Shah, is at the station.
Which of the following best describes how Hannah's detention without charge may be extended?

item.title: Burglary where the intent to steal is formed after entry (Theft Act 1968 s.9(1)(b))
item.description:
During a storm, Marcus Reid walks into his neighbour's house through an open back door to shelter from the rain. He knows he has no permission to be there. When he enters, he intends only to stay dry. Once inside, he sees a laptop on the kitchen table, decides to take it, and leaves with it, intending to sell it. The neighbour, Joanne Fisher, never gave him permission to enter or to take anything.
Which of the following best describes Marcus's liability for burglary?

item.title: Statutory power of advancement: up to the whole presumptive share (Trustee Act 1925 s.32)
item.description:
Grace Adebayo died in 2021. Her will left £300,000 on trust for such of her three grandchildren, Leo, Mia and Noah, as reach 25, in equal shares. The will gives no one a prior life interest and does not exclude or vary the statutory powers. Leo is 19 and has asked the trustees, Peter Clarke and Hannah Liu, for £100,000 of capital as a deposit on a flat. The trustees think this would be for his benefit. Mia and Noah, both adults, object to the payment.
Which of the following best describes the trustees' power under section 32 of the Trustee Act 1925?

item.title: Legal leases of seven years or less as overriding interests (LRA 2002 Sch 3 para 1)
item.description:
Rhys Morgan is the registered proprietor of a freehold yard containing several lock-up units. In February 2026 he granted Amara Bello a six-year lease of one unit by deed, taking effect immediately, at a market rent. The lease was not registered or noted on Rhys's title. Amara uses the unit to store stock and visits it only occasionally; when it was inspected, the unit was padlocked and there was no sign of use. In September 2026 Rhys sold the freehold to Callum Price for value, and Callum was registered as proprietor. Callum had no actual knowledge of Amara's lease.
Which of the following best describes whether Callum is bound by Amara's lease?

item.title: Client account reconciliations every five weeks (SRA Accounts Rules, rule 8.3)
item.description:
Ashby Lane Solicitors LLP holds a general client account and two separate designated deposit client accounts holding large sums for estates in long-running administrations. The firm's cashier, Gareth Pryce, reconciles the general client account every two months by comparing the bank statement balance with the cash book balance. He signs the reconciliation himself. He does not reconcile the designated deposit accounts at all, because he says the money in them rarely moves. The firm's COFA, Leila Haddad, asks what the SRA Accounts Rules require.
Which of the following best describes the firm's obligation?

item.title: Gift to a child who dies before the testator leaving issue (Wills Act 1837 s.33)
item.description:
Margaret Hughes made a valid will in 2019 leaving "£40,000 to my son Owen" and the residue of her estate to her friend Bernadette Kaur. The will contains no other relevant provisions. Owen died in March 2025, leaving a widow, Chloe, and two children, Ella (aged 15) and Sam (aged 21). By his own will Owen left everything to Chloe. Margaret died in September 2026, survived by Chloe, Ella, Sam and Bernadette.
Which of the following best describes who is entitled to the £40,000 legacy?

item.title: Landlord's section 25 notice: timing, termination date and grounds of opposition (LTA 1954 s.25)
item.description:
Harbourside Retail Parks Ltd is the landlord of a shop let to Owain Rees for a fixed term of ten years expiring on 30 June 2027. The lease is not contracted out, and Owain occupies the shop for his bakery business, so Part II of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954 applies. Harbourside intends to demolish and rebuild the parade and does not want to grant Owain a new lease. On 2 December 2026 its solicitor plans to serve a notice under section 25 specifying 30 June 2027 as the date of termination.
Which of the following best describes the requirements for Harbourside's section 25 notice?

item.title: Oral undertakings and the time for performance (SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, para 1.3)
item.description:
Tomasz Wilk, a solicitor, acts for the seller of a house. Shortly before exchange of contracts, the buyer's solicitor, Funmi Okafor, telephones him about a missing building regulations completion certificate. Tomasz says: "Leave it with me. I will send you the certificate as soon as the council issues it to us." No date is mentioned and nothing is put in writing. Relying on this, Funmi advises her client to exchange. The council issues the certificate to Tomasz's firm a week after completion, but four months later Tomasz has still not sent it, as he has been busy with other matters.
Which of the following best describes Tomasz's position under the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors?

item.title: Passing a Bill without the consent of the House of Lords (Parliament Act 1911 s.2, as amended by the Parliament Act 1949)
item.description:
The Government introduces a Local Transport Bill in the House of Commons. It is not a Money Bill and contains nothing about the length of Parliaments. The Bill receives its Commons second reading, passes the Commons and is sent to the House of Lords several months before the end of the session, but the Lords vote it down. In the next session an identical Bill is introduced, passes the Commons and is again sent to the Lords well over a month before the session ends. The Lords reject it a second time. The Commons has not directed that the Parliament Acts should not apply.
Which of the following best describes when the Bill may be presented for Royal Assent without the consent of the House of Lords?

item.title: Using Hansard to interpret a statute: the conditions in Pepper v Hart [1993] AC 593
item.description:
In a High Court claim heard in October 2026, the parties dispute the meaning of a phrase in a section of a 2019 Act. The judge accepts that the phrase is genuinely ambiguous and can reasonably bear either party's reading. Counsel for the claimant wishes to rely on two passages from Hansard: a speech at second reading by a backbench MP, Ruth Adeyemi, giving her own view of what the phrase meant, and an answer in committee by the minister promoting the Bill, which clearly and directly stated which of the two meanings the phrase was intended to have.
Which of the following best describes the extent to which the court may consider this Parliamentary material?

item.title: Occupiers' duty to trespassers and no recovery for property damage (Occupiers' Liability Act 1984 s.1(3), (4) and (8))
item.description:
Brightwell Homes Ltd occupies a fenced building site. Its security reports show that, for several weeks, young adults have been climbing through a gap in the fence at night to use the site as a shortcut, and the company has done nothing about it. One evening in May 2026 workers left a deep trench uncovered and unlit across the usual route, with no warning sign. Marcus Bell, aged 22, climbed through the gap in the dark, fell into the trench and broke his leg. His mobile phone was smashed in the fall.
Which of the following best describes Brightwell Homes Ltd's potential liability to Marcus?

item.title: Excluding liability for negligence in a business contract (Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 s.2)
item.description:
Agnieszka Nowak runs a bakery as a sole trader. In January 2026 she signed Ovenserve Ltd's standard terms for an annual service of her commercial oven. Clause 9 states: "Ovenserve shall not be liable for any death, personal injury, loss or damage of any kind, however caused, including by its negligence." In June 2026 an Ovenserve engineer negligently refitted a gas valve. The next morning the oven caught fire, burning Agnieszka's arm and destroying £3,000 of stock. Ovenserve relies on clause 9 and points out that Agnieszka read and signed the terms.
Which of the following best describes the effect of clause 9 under the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977?

item.title: Claimant fails to beat a defendant's Part 36 offer: costs consequences (CPR 36.17(1)(a) and (3))
item.description:
Northfield Packaging Ltd sued Arden Logistics Ltd for £180,000 damages for breach of contract. On 3 March 2026 Arden served a written offer of £95,000 expressly made under Part 36, stating a relevant period of 21 days. Northfield did not accept it and the offer was never withdrawn or changed. After a trial in September 2026, the judge awarded Northfield £88,000 (inclusive of interest on the same basis as the offer). Northfield's director argues that, as it won the case and the award is close to the offer, the offer should make no difference to costs.
Which of the following best describes the order the court must make, unless it considers it unjust to do so?

item.title: Substantial property transactions with a director: members' approval (CA 2006 ss.190-191)
item.description:
Kestrel Joinery Ltd is a private company whose shares are held equally by three individuals, including Daniel Osei, who is also one of its two directors. The company's most recent statutory accounts show net assets of £400,000. Daniel owns a nearly new delivery van, valued at £45,000, which he has agreed to sell to the company for that price. The other director is happy with the deal and wants to sign the purchase agreement at a board meeting next week, after Daniel has declared his interest. The company's articles contain no relevant special provisions.
Which of the following best describes what the Companies Act 2006 requires before Kestrel Joinery Ltd buys the van?

item.title: Adverse inferences from silence and access to legal advice (CJPOA 1994 s.34(2A))
item.description:
Kwame is arrested on suspicion of assault occasioning actual bodily harm after a fight outside a nightclub and taken to a police station, where he asks to speak to a solicitor. A superintendent authorises a delay in his access to legal advice, and officers interview him under caution before he has had any opportunity to consult a solicitor. Kwame answers 'no comment' to every question. At his trial, he gives evidence that he acted in self-defence. The prosecution invites the court to draw an adverse inference from his failure to mention self-defence in interview.
Which of the following best describes whether an adverse inference may be drawn under s.34 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994?

item.title: Oblique intention and the virtual certainty direction (R v Woollin)
item.description:
Darren owns a shop in Leicester with a flat above it, let to Mrs Okafor, whose only way out is through the shop. Intending to make a fraudulent insurance claim, Darren sets fire to the shop at 3am, knowing that Mrs Okafor is asleep upstairs. He says he hoped she would wake and escape. She dies in the fire, and Darren is charged with murder. In summing up, the trial judge directs the jury that they may find the necessary intention if they are sure that Darren realised there was a substantial risk that the fire would cause death or serious injury.
Which of the following is the correct direction the judge should have given on intention?

item.title: Certainty of intention and precatory words
item.description:
Eleanor died last year. Her will, which is valid, leaves £60,000 'to my sister Joan absolutely, in the hope and confidence that she will use it as she sees fit for the benefit of my nephews, Callum and Rory'. Nothing else in the will refers to the gift or to the nephews. Joan has told Callum and Rory that she plans to spend the money on a round-the-world cruise. They wish to argue that Joan holds the £60,000 on trust for them.
Which of the following best describes Joan's entitlement to the £60,000?

item.title: Overreaching on payment to two trustees and a beneficiary in actual occupation (LPA 1925 ss.2 and 27; City of London BS v Flegg)
item.description:
Hamid and Rania are the registered proprietors of a freehold house in Reading. Rania's mother, Margaret, contributed a third of the purchase price on the understanding that she would have a share in the house, and she has lived there with them ever since. There is no entry on the register referring to Margaret's interest. Without telling Margaret, Hamid and Rania grant a legal charge of the house to Northgate Bank plc, which pays the loan to both of them jointly. The bank makes no enquiry of Margaret. Hamid and Rania have defaulted, and the bank seeks possession. Margaret argues that her beneficial interest binds the bank.
Which of the following best describes Margaret's position against the bank?

item.title: Client account must not be used as a banking facility (SRA Accounts Rules, rule 3.3)
item.description:
Hartley & Rowe LLP acted for Tomasz on the sale of the freehold premises of his former café. Completion took place last week and the firm still holds the £40,000 balance of the sale proceeds in client account. Its bill has been paid. Tomasz is between bank accounts and asks the firm to keep the money in client account for the next six months and, on his instructions, pay his household bills, his suppliers' invoices for a new business and his daughter's university fees.
Which of the following best describes how the firm should respond?

item.title: Revocation of a will by marriage and the expectation of marriage exception (Wills Act 1837 s.18)
item.description:
In 2024, Marcus made a valid will leaving his whole estate to his fiancee, Leila Haddad. The will states: 'I make this will in expectation of my marriage to Leila Haddad and I intend that it shall not be revoked by that marriage.' Marcus and Leila later separated without marrying. In 2026 Marcus married Sofia Brennan. He made no further will and has recently died. Leila claims the estate under the 2024 will.
Which of the following best describes the status of the 2024 will?

item.title: Failure to complete and the notice to complete (SCS 5th ed, condition 6.8)
item.description:
Aisha is selling her flat in Croydon to Ben. The contract incorporates the Standard Conditions of Sale (Fifth Edition, 2018 Revision) without amendment, except for a special condition under which Ben paid a deposit of 5% of the purchase price on exchange. Completion was due on a Monday, but Ben's lender failed to release the mortgage funds and he did not complete. Aisha is ready, able and willing to complete. At 10am on the Tuesday, Aisha's solicitor hand-delivers a notice to complete to the office of Ben's solicitor.
Which of the following best describes the effect of the notice to complete?

item.title: Acting against a former client whose confidential information you hold (SRA Code paras 6.3-6.5)
item.description:
Two years ago Omar, a solicitor at Ashby Cole LLP, advised Lyndon Ltd on refinancing its debts and learned detailed confidential information about its cash flow and lenders. That retainer has ended. Petra Hale now asks the firm to act for her in a claim against Lyndon Ltd for an unpaid debt, and Lyndon's ability to pay is likely to be central to her tactics. The firm still holds Lyndon's file, and the information on it is material to Petra's matter. Petra says she is happy to sign anything to get Omar's help.
Which of the following best describes whether Ashby Cole LLP may act for Petra?

item.title: Effect of a declaration of incompatibility (HRA 1998 ss.3-4)
item.description:
In proceedings in the High Court, Farah Siddiqui argues that a section of an Act of Parliament breaches her right to respect for private and family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The judge concludes that the provision cannot be read and given effect in a way that is compatible with Article 8, and makes a declaration of incompatibility.
Which of the following best describes the effect of the declaration?

item.title: Court of Appeal and its own previous decisions (Young v Bristol Aeroplane)
item.description:
In 2026 the Court of Appeal (Civil Division) hears an appeal in which the respondent, Callum Reid, relies on a 2019 decision of a three-judge Court of Appeal that is directly in point. The appellant, Seren Price, shows that in 2019 the court was not referred to, and plainly did not have in mind, a rule having statutory force which governs the point and points the other way. Because of the importance of the issue, a five-judge court has been convened. There is no relevant decision of the House of Lords or Supreme Court.
Which of the following best describes whether the Court of Appeal may decline to follow its 2019 decision?

item.title: Secondary victims after Paul v Royal Wolverhampton NHS Trust
item.description:
In March, Dr Okafor negligently failed to diagnose Daniel's serious heart disease when Daniel attended his GP surgery with chest pain. Eight months later, Daniel suffered a cardiac arrest at home and collapsed in front of his wife, Mei, who watched paramedics try and fail to resuscitate him. Mei has since been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder. It is accepted that Daniel would have survived with proper treatment, that Mei and Daniel had a close and loving marriage, and that a person of reasonable fortitude in Mei's position might have suffered a psychiatric illness.
Which of the following best describes whether Mei can recover damages as a secondary victim?

item.title: Part payment of a debt (Foakes v Beer)
item.description:
Gareth, a self-employed joiner, invoiced Ruth £8,000 for fitted wardrobes. The work is not disputed and payment was due on 1 June. Ruth, who could have paid in full, knew that Gareth urgently needed cash to pay his own suppliers. On 1 June she told him: "I will pay you £5,000 if you accept it in full settlement. If you don't, you'll get nothing." Gareth reluctantly signed a note, not executed as a deed, accepting £5,000 "in full and final settlement", and Ruth paid £5,000 by bank transfer that day. Two weeks later Gareth's solicitor wrote demanding the £3,000 balance.
Which of the following best describes whether Gareth can recover the £3,000?

item.title: Default judgment after an acknowledgment of service (CPR 10.3, 15.4, 12.3)
item.description:
Marsh Electrical Ltd issues a claim for a specified sum of £48,000 for unpaid invoices against Harlow Fabrication Ltd. The claim form and particulars of claim are served together. Harlow files an acknowledgment of service within the time allowed, stating that it intends to defend the whole claim. No extension of time has been agreed or ordered. Sixteen days after service of the particulars of claim, no defence has been filed, and Marsh's trainee suggests filing a request for default judgment straight away.
Which of the following best describes the position?

item.title: Declaring an interest in a proposed transaction (CA 2006 s.177)
item.description:
Priya Nair is one of four directors of Halden Interiors Ltd. The board plans to approve a five-year lease of a warehouse from Moorgate Holdings Ltd at its meeting next week. Priya's husband owns 60% of the shares in Moorgate Holdings Ltd. None of the other directors knows of this, and Priya has said nothing because she personally holds no shares in Moorgate and will not be signing the lease.
Which of the following best describes Priya's duty under the Companies Act 2006?

item.title: Delaying access to legal advice at the police station (PACE s.58)
item.description:
Kemi is arrested on suspicion of burglary of a warehouse and taken to a police station, where she asks to speak to a solicitor. The police believe two accomplices have not yet been arrested. An inspector authorises a delay in Kemi's access to a solicitor, on the ground that a solicitor's call might alert the accomplices.
Which of the following best describes whether the delay is lawful?

item.title: The test for dishonesty after Ivey v Genting and R v Barton
item.description:
Leon, a self-employed builder, finishes a kitchen refit for a client and sends an invoice that includes £900 for materials he knows he never bought or used. He is charged with fraud by false representation. In interview he says that 'everyone in the trade pads their invoices' and that he did not think anyone would regard it as dishonest.
Which of the following best describes how the court will decide whether Leon acted dishonestly?

item.title: The rule in Saunders v Vautier: ending a trust early
item.description:
By her will, Sofia's grandmother left £60,000 to trustees 'on trust for my granddaughter Sofia absolutely, but the trustees shall not pay the capital to her until she reaches the age of 25; until then the income is to be accumulated and added to the capital.' Sofia is now 19, has full mental capacity, and asks the trustees to transfer the whole fund to her. No one else has any interest under the trust.
Which of the following best describes Sofia's position?

item.title: Freehold covenants: the burden of a positive covenant does not run
item.description:
In 2012 Ivy sold part of her registered freehold land to Ben. In the transfer Ivy covenanted, for herself and her successors in title, to maintain the boundary fence between the two plots. In 2020 Ivy sold her retained land to Carl. Carl claims no right or benefit under the 2012 transfer. The fence has now collapsed, and Carl refuses to repair it. Ben wants to sue Carl.
Which of the following best describes whether Ben can enforce the covenant against Carl?

item.title: Transferring client money for costs: bill first (SRA Accounts Rules 4.3)
item.description:
A firm acting for a client on the purchase of a house holds £3,000 in client account, received from the client 'on account of costs' at the start of the matter. The fee earner has now done work worth £1,200 plus VAT (£1,440 in total). She wants the cashier to transfer £1,440 to the business (office) account today and plans to send the client a bill next week.
Which of the following best describes what the firm must do before transferring the money?

item.title: Intestacy and the 28-day spousal survivorship rule
item.description:
Arjun died intestate on 1 May 2026, domiciled in England. He was survived by his wife, Neha, and their two adult children. Neha was seriously ill and died 19 days after Arjun. Arjun's estate consists of personal chattels and investments well in excess of the statutory legacy.
Which of the following best describes how Arjun's estate will be distributed?

item.title: Gifts to a witness's spouse under section 15 Wills Act 1837
item.description:
Rosalind signed her will in the presence of two witnesses: her neighbour, Priti, and Gareth, the husband of her close friend Lena. Gareth and Lena were married at the time. The will leaves £20,000 to Lena and the residue to Rosalind's nephew. No one else witnessed the will. Rosalind has now died, and the will was otherwise validly executed.
Which of the following best describes the effect of Gareth having witnessed the will?

item.title: Priority period of an official search of registered land (OS1)
item.description:
A solicitor acts for a buyer of a registered freehold house, with a mortgage. Before completion she applies for an official search of the whole of the title with priority (form OS1), and the result reveals no adverse entries. Completion takes place a week later.
Which of the following best describes the protection the official search gives the buyer?

item.title: Acting for clients competing for the same objective (SRA Code 6.2)
item.description:
Two long-standing clients of a commercial property firm, Harbour Coffee Ltd and Kiln Bakery Ltd, separately ask the firm to act for them in bidding for the lease of the same high-street unit. The landlord's agent is running a sealed-bid process and only one lease will be granted. Both clients want to keep using the firm.
Which of the following best describes whether the firm may act for both clients?

item.title: Judicial review time limits: promptly and within three months
item.description:
On 2 March 2026 a local council revoked Bilal's street-trading licence. The decision has nothing to do with planning. Bilal instructs a solicitor in late May 2026. He has a letter from the council's legal department saying that the council 'will not take any point on delay' provided any judicial review claim is filed by 31 July 2026.
Which of the following best describes the time limit for Bilal's claim for judicial review?

item.title: Pre-incorporation contracts: personal liability of the person acting (CA 2006 s.51)
item.description:
Imogen and Rafael plan to run a kitchen showroom through a new private company, Brightwater Kitchens Ltd. Before the company is registered at Companies House, Imogen signs an order with a supplier for display units worth £18,000, signing "for and on behalf of Brightwater Kitchens Ltd". Nothing in the order deals with who is to be liable if the company has not been formed. The company is incorporated three weeks later, but no new contract is made with the supplier, which has not been paid. Assume the law of England and Wales applies.
Who is liable to the supplier under the order?

item.title: Written special resolution: 75% of total voting rights of eligible members (CA 2006 ss.21, 283)
item.description:
Larkspur Analytics Ltd is a private company limited by shares with unamended model articles. Its 100 issued ordinary shares each carry one vote and are held by Femi (40), Gwen (25), Hamid (20) and Ines (15). The directors circulate a written resolution, stated to be proposed as a special resolution, to amend the articles. Within the period for agreement, Femi and Gwen signify their agreement, Ines notifies the company that she opposes it, and Hamid does not respond at all.
What is the status of the written resolution?

item.title: Directors authorising a director's conflict of interest in a private company (CA 2006 s.175)
item.description:
Quillon Robotics Ltd is a private company limited by shares with unamended model articles and three directors: Nadia, Oskar and Priyanka. Through her role as a director, Nadia learns of a consultancy contract that the board has decided the company cannot take on because it lacks capacity. Nadia wants to take the contract through her own consultancy business. At a properly convened board meeting she discloses the full facts. Oskar and Priyanka vote to authorise her to take the opportunity. Nadia is present but does not vote and is not counted in the quorum. Nothing in the company's constitution restricts directors' authorisation of conflicts.
Which statement best describes the position on Nadia's conflict?

item.title: Director's service contract over two years without members' approval (CA 2006 ss.188-189)
item.description:
Osterley Freight Ltd is a private company limited by shares; it is not a subsidiary of any other company. Its board alone approves a service contract for the managing director, Tobiah. The contract is for a fixed term of four years and the company cannot terminate it by notice during that term except for gross misconduct. No resolution of the members was ever proposed or passed in relation to the contract. Eighteen months later the board wishes to end Tobiah's employment, although he has committed no misconduct.
What is the effect of the failure to obtain the members' approval?

item.title: Ratifying a director's negligence: votes of the director and connected persons (CA 2006 s.239)
item.description:
Wexcombe Tiles Ltd is a private company limited by shares with 1,000 issued ordinary shares, each carrying one vote. Callum, a director, holds 400 shares. His wife, Mairead, who is not a director, holds 100 shares. The remaining 500 shares are held by three unconnected investors. Callum negligently approved a supply contract that has cost the company £60,000; he received no personal benefit and there is no suggestion of fraud. The board calls a general meeting to propose an ordinary resolution ratifying Callum's conduct. On a poll, Callum and Mairead vote all their shares in favour. Of the investors' shares, 300 are voted in favour and 200 against.
Is the ratification resolution passed?

item.title: Members requiring directors to call a general meeting: timing (CA 2006 ss.303-304)
item.description:
Yusuf holds ordinary shares representing 7% of the paid-up voting share capital of Thornbury Organics Ltd, a private company limited by shares. The directors have ignored his informal suggestions that the shareholders should consider appointing an additional director. Yusuf now sends the company a properly authenticated request that the directors call a general meeting. The request states the general nature of the business and sets out the text of an ordinary resolution to appoint the new director, which may properly be moved.
What must the directors do once the company has received Yusuf's request?

item.title: Excluded minority in a quasi-partnership company: unfair prejudice petition (CA 2006 ss.994, 996)
item.description:
In 2018 three friends formed Marlowe Print Ltd, a private company limited by shares, on the shared understanding that each would be a director and take part in running the business. Each holds one third of the shares. After a falling-out, the other two shareholders validly remove Abena as a director by ordinary resolution after giving special notice, and exclude her from all involvement in management. The company has since paid no dividends, while paying the two remaining directors substantially increased salaries. Abena would like to leave the company and receive a fair value for her shares.
Which course of action is most appropriate for Abena?

item.title: Allotting shares for cash in a single-class private company: s.550 authority and s.569 pre-emption
item.description:
Fenwick & Sloane Ltd was incorporated in 2021. It is a private company limited by shares with only one class of shares (ordinary shares) and unamended model articles. The members have never passed any resolution about the allotment of shares or pre-emption rights. The directors want to allot 500 new ordinary shares to a new investor, Lucía, for £20 each in cash. They do not want to offer the shares to the existing shareholders first.
Which shareholder resolution(s), if any, are needed before the directors can make the allotment to Lucía?

item.title: Off-market buyback by written resolution: majority and seller's eligibility (CA 2006 ss.694-695)
item.description:
Ravensworth Engineering Ltd is a private company limited by shares with unamended model articles, which contain no restriction on the purchase of its own shares. Its 1,000 ordinary shares, each with one vote, are held by Hugo (300), Beatrix (400) and Cyrus (300). Hugo is retiring, and the company has agreed in principle to buy back all of his shares under a contract made directly with him (not on a recognised investment exchange). It has ample distributable profits to fund the price. The directors propose to seek the members' approval of the contract terms by written resolution before the contract is entered into.
Which statement correctly describes the members' approval needed?

item.title: Unlawful dividend: which shareholders must repay (CA 2006 ss.830, 847)
item.description:
Saoirse and Theo each hold 50% of the shares in Kestrel Bakeries Ltd, a private company limited by shares with unamended model articles. Saoirse is the managing director and prepared the company's annual accounts herself. Theo is a passive investor who is not a director and sees only the accounts. On the directors' recommendation, the members declared a final dividend of £50,000 based on those accounts, and each received £25,000. It later emerges that Saoirse knowingly left out a large write-down of obsolete stock. Properly prepared, the accounts would have shown accumulated realised losses and no distributable profits. Theo had no reason to suspect anything was wrong.
Which shareholder, if any, is liable under the Companies Act 2006 to repay the dividend received?

item.title: Failure to register a company charge within 21 days (CA 2006 ss.859A, 859H)
item.description:
Pembury Castings Ltd granted Halden Bank plc a fixed charge over its factory premises to secure a £400,000 loan. Through an oversight, neither the company nor the bank delivered a statement of particulars of the charge to the registrar of companies, and no court order extending the time for delivery was ever sought. Some months later the company goes into insolvent liquidation with the full £400,000 still owing to the bank.
What is the bank's position in the liquidation?

item.title: Order of payment from floating charge realisations in a liquidation (IA 1986 ss.175, 176A)
item.description:
Ashgrove Interiors Ltd is in insolvent liquidation in England. Its bank holds a fixed charge over the company's warehouse and a floating charge over all its other assets, both created in 2019 and properly registered. The warehouse has been sold and the fixed charge proceeds paid to the bank. The liquidator has also realised a substantial sum from the floating charge assets. This sum is not enough to pay everyone in full, and the prescribed part has not been disapplied. The creditors include employees with preferential claims, unsecured trade creditors and the bank for the balance of its debt. The liquidator has also incurred expenses of the winding up.
In what order will the liquidator apply the floating charge realisations?

item.title: Partner's authority to bind the firm despite an internal spending limit (Partnership Act 1890 s.5)
item.description:
Emeka and Signe run a graphic design studio in England as a general partnership under a written partnership agreement. The agreement provides that neither partner may order equipment costing more than £5,000 without the other's consent. Without consulting Signe, Emeka orders a £9,000 large-format printer for the studio from Prism Supplies Ltd. Prism regularly supplies design studios and knows that Emeka is a partner, but it knows nothing about the spending limit in the partnership agreement. Signe refuses to pay for the printer.
Is the firm bound by the contract with Prism Supplies Ltd?

item.title: Retired partner's liability to an existing customer without notice (Partnership Act 1890 s.36)
item.description:
Rowena retired on 30 April from Harrow & Beck, a firm of building contractors in England trading as a general partnership. The firm placed a notice of her retirement in the London Gazette but did not write to its customers or suppliers. Delmont Timber Ltd had supplied the firm regularly for several years and knew Rowena was a partner. In June it supplied £14,000 of timber to the firm on credit. It had not seen the Gazette notice and had received no other notice of the retirement. The firm cannot pay the invoice.
Can Delmont Timber Ltd hold Rowena liable for the June debt?

item.title: LLP carrying on business with one member for more than six months (LLPA 2000 s.4A)
item.description:
Ellery Fold LLP, a limited liability partnership incorporated in England, had two members, Joaquín and Wren. Wren died on 1 January. Fully aware of her death, Joaquín carried on the LLP's business alone for the next ten months without admitting any new member. During that time the LLP incurred a debt of £20,000 to one supplier in February and a debt of £35,000 to another supplier in September. The LLP is now insolvent and both debts are unpaid.
What is Joaquín's personal liability for these debts?

item.title: Repaying a director's loan before liquidation: preference to a connected person (IA 1986 ss.239-240)
item.description:
Corvan Displays Ltd went into insolvent creditors' voluntary liquidation on 1 September 2026. Eighteen months earlier, when it was already unable to pay its debts as they fell due, it repaid in full an unsecured loan of £40,000 made to it by its managing director, Felix, while its trade creditors went unpaid. Felix says the company repaid him only because he had been pressing hard for payment, and not to put him in a better position than other creditors. The liquidator is considering whether the repayment can be challenged.
Can the liquidator challenge the repayment to Felix?

item.title: Floating charge granted to secure an existing overdraft before liquidation (IA 1986 s.245)
item.description:
Larchfield Ltd owed £150,000 to Norbury Bank plc on an unsecured overdraft. The bank is not connected with the company. Worried about the company's finances, the bank froze the account and demanded security. Eight months before the company went into insolvent liquidation, the company granted the bank a floating charge over all its assets to secure the existing overdraft. The bank provided no further money, goods or services after the charge was created, and there were no further payments into or out of the account. The company was unable to pay its debts at the time the charge was created. The charge was registered within 21 days.
What is the status of the floating charge in the liquidation?

item.title: Wrongful trading: the 'every step' defence (IA 1986 s.214)
item.description:
Gaia is a director of Tamsin Lighting Ltd. In March she concluded, as she should have done, that there was no reasonable prospect of the company avoiding insolvent liquidation. The company went into insolvent liquidation in August. The liquidator is considering applying to the court for a declaration that Gaia must contribute to the company's assets for wrongful trading.
Which of the following, if established, would give Gaia a defence?

item.title: Creditors' bankruptcy petition: aggregating debts to reach the bankruptcy level (IA 1986 ss.267-268)
item.description:
Dariusz is a sole trader in England. He owes £3,200 to Mapleton Supplies Ltd and £2,100 to Sefton Hire Ltd. Both debts are unsecured, for liquidated sums and immediately payable. Four weeks ago each creditor served a statutory demand on Dariusz in the prescribed form. Neither demand has been paid, secured or compounded for, and Dariusz has made no application to set either aside. Assume the bankruptcy level is £5,000.
Can a bankruptcy petition be presented against Dariusz?

item.title: Sole trader's loss in the first year of trading: early trade losses relief (ITA 2007 ss.72-73)
item.description:
Marisol was employed as an engineer until 5 April 2026, earning a salary of about £58,000 in each of the tax years 2023/24, 2024/25 and 2025/26. On 6 April 2026 she started trading as a sole trader, on a commercial basis and with a view to profit. She expects a trading loss of £30,000 for 2026/27, her first tax year of trading, and has no other income in that year. She wants to set the loss against her earliest available income. Assume that no cap or other restriction on income tax reliefs limits her claim.
Which relief allows the loss to be set against her 2023/24 employment income, and how does it operate?

item.title: Company trading loss: current-year and 12-month carry-back relief (CTA 2010 s.37)
item.description:
Brackenfield Tools Ltd has traded for many years and prepares accounts to 31 March. In its accounting period ended 31 March 2026 it made a trading loss of £80,000 and a chargeable gain of £20,000, and had no other income. In its accounting period ended 31 March 2025 its total profits were £50,000. The company continues to trade and makes a claim under s.37 Corporation Tax Act 2010 that includes carrying the loss back.
How will the £80,000 loss be relieved?

item.title: Income tax on dividends for a director-shareholder in 2026/27 (ITA 2007 ss.8, 13A)
item.description:
Anjali is a director and shareholder of Pellmar Ltd, a UK trading company. In the tax year 2026/27 she receives a salary of £30,570 and dividends of £30,000 from the company. She has no other income, is entitled to the standard personal allowance and lives in England. Assume the following for 2026/27: personal allowance £12,570; basic rate band £37,700; dividend allowance (dividend nil rate) £500; dividend ordinary rate 10.75%; dividend upper rate 35.75%. Dividends are treated as the top slice of income. Ignore National Insurance.
How much income tax is payable on Anjali's dividends?

item.title: Business Asset Disposal Relief: officer or employee condition not met for two years (CGT)
item.description:
In June 2026 Ottilie sells her entire 12% shareholding in Hartwell Trading Ltd, an unquoted trading company, making a chargeable gain of £400,000. Her shares carry 12% of the voting rights and entitle her to 12% of distributable profits and of assets on a winding up. She bought the shares from another shareholder in 2019 as a passive investor, and was first appointed as a director of the company in March 2025. She is a higher rate taxpayer, makes no other disposals in 2026/27 and has never claimed Business Asset Disposal Relief. Assume: annual exempt amount £3,000; CGT rate for higher rate taxpayers 24%; Business Asset Disposal Relief rate 18% (lifetime limit £1 million). No other relief is available.
How much capital gains tax is payable on the disposal?

item.title: Gift of unquoted trading company shares: hold-over relief and donee's base cost (TCGA 1992 s.165)
item.description:
In 2026/27 Bernard gives his daughter Lowri ordinary shares in Tidemill Joinery Ltd, an unquoted trading company. The shares have a market value of £300,000 at the date of the gift, and Bernard's allowable base cost is £50,000. Bernard and Lowri both sign a claim for gift relief under s.165 Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992. Ignore the annual exempt amount and any other relief.
What is the capital gains tax effect of the gift and the claim?

item.title: Inheritance tax business property relief: two-year minimum ownership
item.description:
Leopold died on 1 September 2026. Twenty months before his death, he bought for cash a 25% shareholding in Caraway Foods Ltd, an unquoted company that carries on a food manufacturing trade. The shares did not replace any other business property, and he did not inherit them from a spouse. At his death the shares were worth £400,000. Assume that any cap on the amount of 100% relief is not relevant because the value is well within it.
Is business property relief available on the shares in Leopold's estate?

item.title: VAT registration threshold: zero-rated supplies count, exempt supplies do not
item.description:
Sunniva runs a business in England and is not registered for VAT. In the 12 months to 31 August 2026 her sales were: £70,000 of standard-rated supplies, £18,000 of zero-rated supplies and £9,000 of exempt supplies. She does not expect her taxable turnover to exceed the threshold in the next 30 days. Assume the VAT registration threshold is £90,000.
Is Sunniva required to register for VAT?

item.title: Goods on display in a self-service shop: invitation to treat (Boots)
item.description:
Imani Okafor, an adult, takes a cordless drill from a shelf in a DIY store in England. The shelf label wrongly shows the price as £19 instead of £119. She puts the drill in her basket and takes it to the till. The cashier notices the error and says the store will only sell the drill for £119. Imani insists that a contract was made at £19 when she placed the drill in her basket.
Which of the following best describes the legal position?

item.title: Acceptance by post and an offeror who sells elsewhere before the letter arrives
item.description:
On 2 March Gwen Pryce, who runs a stables in England, writes to Tariq Haddad offering to sell him a horsebox for £9,500 and asking him to reply by post. Tariq receives the letter on 4 March and the same day posts a properly addressed and stamped letter accepting the offer. On 5 March, before Tariq's letter arrives, Gwen sells the horsebox to someone else. She sends Tariq no message withdrawing her offer. Tariq's letter reaches her on 6 March.
Which of the following best describes the legal position?

item.title: Extra pay for performing an existing contractual duty: practical benefit (Williams v Roffey)
item.description:
Brightwell Construction Ltd is main contractor on a school extension in England. It sub-contracted the roofing to Kofi Asante for £40,000. Halfway through, Brightwell's site manager realised Kofi had underpriced the job and might not be able to finish. Brightwell faces a large delay payment under its main contract if the roof is late. On Brightwell's own initiative, its manager promised Kofi an extra £6,000 if he completed the roof on time. Kofi did not threaten to stop work. He completed on time, but Brightwell now refuses to pay the £6,000, saying Kofi only did what he was already bound to do.
Which of the following best describes whether Kofi can recover the £6,000?

item.title: Intention to create legal relations between spouses who have separated (Merritt v Merritt)
item.description:
Daniel and Rosa Ferreira married in 2009. In March 2026 Daniel moved out of the family home in England to live with a new partner, and the couple agreed to separate. At a meeting a week later, after long discussion, Daniel signed a note: "In return for you paying off the remaining £4,000 loan on the family car, I will pay you £600 a month towards your living costs." Rosa paid off the car loan from her own earnings. Daniel paid nothing and now says the note was a family arrangement with no legal effect.
Which of the following best describes whether the agreement is legally binding?

item.title: Goods delivered with no agreed price: reasonable price (Sale of Goods Act 1979 s.8)
item.description:
Oakmere Garden Centre Ltd telephoned Hollins Timber Ltd and ordered 200 fence panels for delivery the following week. Nothing was said about price, and the two companies had never traded before. Hollins delivered the panels and Oakmere has sold most of them. Hollins has now invoiced Oakmere at its own list price, which is well above the usual market price. Oakmere argues there was never a binding contract because the price was not agreed.
Which of the following best describes Oakmere's liability under the Sale of Goods Act 1979?

item.title: A minor's liability for necessaries (Sale of Goods Act 1979 s.3)
item.description:
Callum Reid, aged 17, has just started an apprenticeship with a building firm in England. He has no safety boots or waterproof work jacket, both of which he needs for site work. He buys a pair of safety boots and a work jacket from a workwear shop on account for £400, which is £150 more than the usual price of such items. They are delivered to him and he wears them at work. He has not paid, and the shop sues him for £400.
Which of the following best describes Callum's liability?

item.title: Third party enforcing a term that benefits them (Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 s.1)
item.description:
Hannah Clarke engages Ridgeway Builders Ltd to build a garden wall at her home in England for £8,000. Because the work will disturb her neighbour, the written contract includes a term: "Ridgeway will also repaint the boundary fence of Mr Leon Baptiste of 14 Elm Road at no extra charge." Nothing in the contract says who may enforce its terms or suggests that the parties did not intend Leon to enforce this one. Ridgeway builds the wall but refuses to repaint Leon's fence. Hannah is not interested in pursuing it.
Which of the following best describes whether Leon can enforce the fence-painting term against Ridgeway?

item.title: Varying a contract after the third party has communicated assent (C(RTP)A 1999 s.2)
item.description:
Rafael Costa pays Lakeside Travel Ltd £3,200 for a week's cruise for his mother, Maria Costa, who is named in the contract as the passenger. The contract states that Maria may enforce its terms and contains no provision about later variation. Lakeside sends Maria the booking details and she emails Lakeside: "Thank you, I accept and am delighted." A month later Rafael and Lakeside agree to transfer the booking to Rafael's brother instead. Maria has not been asked and objects. She has not yet spent any money in reliance on the cruise.
Which of the following best describes the effect of the agreement to transfer the booking?

item.title: Exclusion notice displayed after the contract is made at an automatic car park barrier (Thornton)
item.description:
Sanjay Mehta drove to a multi-storey car park in England. At the entrance, a sign showed only the hourly charges. He pulled up to an automatic barrier, which issued a ticket stating "Issued subject to the conditions displayed inside" and lifted. Having driven in, he passed a notice on a pillar inside stating that the operator accepts no liability for damage to vehicles, however caused. Sanjay did not read the ticket or the notice. While parked, his car was damaged by the operator's negligence. The operator relies on the notice.
Leaving aside any statutory controls on exclusion clauses, which of the following best describes whether the exclusion clause is part of the contract?

item.title: Implying a term in fact: necessity or obviousness, not fairness (M&S v BNP Paribas)
item.description:
Under a detailed written licence negotiated by solicitors, Pennant Media Ltd pays Carrick Studios Ltd an annual fee of £60,000 in advance each January for exclusive use of a recording studio in England. Clause 14 allows Pennant to end the licence on one month's written notice at any time. The licence says nothing about refunding any part of the annual fee if Pennant ends the licence part-way through a year. Pennant gives notice ending the licence on 31 March and claims a refund for April to December, arguing that a term to that effect must be implied because it would be fair.
Which of the following best describes the approach a court will take to Pennant's argument?

item.title: Interpreting a clear price escalation clause that became a bad bargain (Arnold v Britton)
item.description:
In 2016 Fenwick Logistics Ltd signed a ten-year warehouse management contract with Delta Stores Ltd, both companies taking legal advice. Clause 5 states: "The annual fee shall be £200,000 in the first year and shall increase by 8% each year, compounded." Inflation has since been much lower than either party expected, and the fee now far exceeds market rates. Delta argues that commercial common sense requires clause 5 to be read as an increase of 8% or the rate of inflation, whichever is lower.
Which of the following best describes how a court is likely to interpret clause 5?

item.title: Slight breach of an implied condition in a business sale (Sale of Goods Act 1979 s.15A)
item.description:
Larkspur Catering Ltd buys 500 aprons from Tidewell Textiles Ltd for use in its restaurants in England. The contract describes them as "navy blue, 100% cotton". The aprons delivered are 100% cotton but a very slightly lighter shade of navy than the sample in Tidewell's catalogue, a difference noticeable only when they are laid side by side. They are perfectly usable. Larkspur, which has found a cheaper supplier, wants to reject the whole delivery for breach of the implied term that goods correspond with their description. The contract says nothing about remedies.
Which of the following best describes Larkspur's position?

item.title: Excluding liability for satisfactory quality in a consumer sale (Consumer Rights Act 2015 s.31)
item.description:
Bethan Lloyd buys a new washing machine for her home from Sparkle Appliances Ltd, a retailer in England. Sparkle's order form, which Bethan signs, states in bold: "Goods sold as seen. Sparkle accepts no liability for any fault in the goods." Within a week the drum stops turning because of a manufacturing defect. Sparkle says Bethan agreed to the clause and refuses to do anything.
Which of the following best describes the effect of the clause?

item.title: Oral variation of a contract containing a 'No Oral Modification' clause (Rock Advertising)
item.description:
Northgate Office Space Ltd licensed serviced offices in England to Quill Design Ltd for two years at £5,000 a month. Clause 11 of the signed written licence states: "This licence may only be varied in writing signed by both parties." When Quill fell into arrears, Northgate's credit manager agreed with Quill's director in a phone call to accept £3,000 a month for six months, with the shortfall spread over the rest of the term. Nothing was put in writing. Northgate's director has now refused to honour the arrangement and claims the full contractual rent. Assume no argument based on estoppel arises.
Which of the following best describes the effect of the telephone agreement?

item.title: Court's discretion to award damages in lieu of rescission (Misrepresentation Act 1967 s.2(2))
item.description:
In May 2026 Harrowby Print Ltd bought a used printing press for £85,000 from Selwyn Graphics Ltd. Before the sale, Selwyn's manager told Harrowby the press had been made in 2019. He honestly believed this, relying on the manufacturer's service records, which turned out to contain a clerical error. The press was in fact made in 2018. It works perfectly and its value is only about £2,000 lower than that of a 2019 model. Harrowby discovered the truth two weeks after delivery, at once asked to rescind, and has since issued proceedings claiming rescission. No bar to rescission has arisen.
Which of the following best describes the court's powers in Harrowby's claim?

item.title: Sale of specific goods that had already perished (Sale of Goods Act 1979 s.6)
item.description:
On Monday morning Ashby Fine Wines Ltd agreed to sell to Marlow Hotels Ltd a specific consignment of 40 identified cases of a particular vintage claret stored in a named bonded warehouse in England, for £24,000. Unknown to either party, the warehouse had been destroyed by fire overnight and all 40 cases were lost. Marlow has paid nothing. Ashby says Marlow must pay because risk passed when the contract was made.
Which of the following best describes the legal position?

item.title: Economic duress: the requirement of no reasonable alternative (PIA v Times Travel)
item.description:
Corbett Bakeries Ltd has a fixed-price contract with Glenmoor Mills Ltd for weekly deliveries of flour to its bakery in England. Midway through the term, Glenmoor tells Corbett it will stop delivering unless Corbett agrees a 15% price rise. Glenmoor has no right under the contract to do this. Corbett's buyer knows that two other mills in the area could supply the same flour at the original price from the next day, but finds it simpler to sign Glenmoor's revised price schedule. Corbett now wants to set the price variation aside for economic duress.
Which of the following best describes whether Corbett is likely to succeed?

item.title: Undue influence and a joint loan to spouses: when the lender is put on inquiry (CIBC v Pitt)
item.description:
Martin and Aisha Kendall jointly own their home in England. Martin pressured Aisha, against her wishes, into agreeing to remortgage it; a court would find this was actual undue influence. Both applied to Harbour Bank plc for a joint loan of £120,000, stated on the application to be for home improvements and a holiday flat for the family. The bank had no knowledge of Martin's conduct, did not use him as its agent, and paid the loan into the couple's joint account. Martin secretly spent the money on his own failed business. The bank now seeks possession, and Aisha argues that the charge cannot be enforced against her.
Which of the following best describes the position between Aisha and the bank?

item.title: Recovering money paid for an unlawful purpose (Patel v Mirza)
item.description:
Ollie Grant paid £25,000 to his friend Dev Rana, a trader, so that Dev could place bets on the share price of a listed company using inside information Dev expected to receive. Both knew that dealing on inside information is a criminal offence. The expected information never came, Dev placed no bets, and he has refused to return the money. Ollie sues Dev in England to recover the £25,000.
Which of the following best describes whether Ollie can recover the £25,000?

item.title: Sums paid and payable before frustration, and expenses (LR(FC)A 1943 s.1(2))
item.description:
Ngozi Eze hired Fairfield Hall in England for her wedding reception on 20 July 2026 for a total fee of £10,000. Under the contract she paid a £4,000 deposit in January. A further £3,000 was due on 1 June, but she had not paid it. On 10 June the hall was destroyed by fire without fault on either side, and it is agreed that the contract was frustrated. Before the fire the hall's owner had spent £1,500 in preparing for the event. The contract makes no provision for what happens if the hall cannot be used.
Which of the following best describes the position under the Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943?

item.title: Remoteness: losses from special circumstances not communicated (Hadley v Baxendale)
item.description:
Wren Valley Dairy Ltd, a cheese maker in England, sent product samples by Swiftline Couriers Ltd for next-day delivery to a laboratory. Wren Valley did not tell Swiftline that the samples had to reach the laboratory that day so that test results could be sent to a foreign buyer before a deadline in a £60,000 export deal. Swiftline delivered three days late through its own fault. Wren Valley had to pay £300 for a second, express delivery of fresh samples, and lost the export deal because the deadline passed.
Which of the following best describes the damages Wren Valley can recover from Swiftline?

item.title: Liquidated damages or penalty: the legitimate interest test (Cavendish v Makdessi)
item.description:
Vantage Software Ltd agreed to install a booking system for Coastal Ferries Ltd by 1 March 2026. Clause 9 provides that if installation is late, Vantage will pay Coastal £50,000 for each day of delay. Both companies took legal advice. Coastal's realistic loss from delay is at most about £2,000 a day, and Coastal has identified no other commercial interest that the clause protects. Installation was completed ten days late, and Coastal claims £500,000 under clause 9.
Which of the following best describes whether clause 9 is enforceable?

item.title: Specific performance of a covenant to keep a business open (Co-operative Insurance v Argyll)
item.description:
Brackley Retail Park Ltd let the largest unit on its retail park in England to Pulse Fitness Ltd for 25 years. The lease contains a covenant by Pulse "to keep the premises open as a gym during normal trading hours". The gym has been losing money and Pulse has closed it, in deliberate breach of covenant, while it looks for someone to take over the lease. Brackley says the closure is reducing visitor numbers to other shops on the park and seeks an order compelling Pulse to reopen and run the gym.
Which of the following best describes how the court is likely to respond?

item.title: Oral guarantee of another's debt (Statute of Frauds 1677 s.4)
item.description:
Kestrel Packaging Ltd supplies boxes on credit to Mill Lane Bakery Ltd. When Mill Lane fell behind with payments, Kestrel threatened to stop supplying. Mill Lane's managing director, Ahmed Siddiqui, told Kestrel's sales manager in a phone call: "Keep supplying us. If the company doesn't pay you, I personally will." Nothing was written down or signed. Kestrel kept supplying, Mill Lane has now gone into liquidation owing £18,000, and Kestrel sues Ahmed personally.
Which of the following best describes whether Kestrel can enforce Ahmed's promise against him?

item.title: Lump sum contract substantially performed with minor defects (Hoenig v Isaacs)
item.description:
Lucia Romano, an interior designer, agreed to design and fit out a studio flat in England for Owen Blake for a lump sum of £15,000, payable "£5,000 on starting, balance on completion". She completed all the work and Owen moved in and has used the furniture and fittings since. A built-in bookcase is 5 cm too short and a wardrobe door is warped; putting both right will cost £900. Owen has paid only the first £5,000 and refuses to pay anything more, saying Lucia has not performed the contract.
Which of the following best describes Owen's liability?

item.title: Liability for failing to act after creating a dangerous situation (R v Miller duty)
item.description:
Tomasz Nowak, an adult, is staying overnight at his friend Ellen's flat in Leeds. He lights a candle on a bookshelf and falls asleep on the sofa. He wakes to find that the candle has set the curtain smouldering and realises the fire may spread. Annoyed and tired, he goes into the spare room and back to sleep without trying to put the fire out or raising the alarm. The fire spreads and badly damages Ellen's living room. He is charged with arson (Criminal Damage Act 1971, s.1(1) and (3)). He says he did not intend or foresee any damage when he lit the candle.
Which of the following best describes whether Tomasz can be criminally liable for the damage caused by the fire?

item.title: Subjective recklessness in criminal damage (R v G)
item.description:
Priya Shah, aged 19, and a friend shelter behind a warehouse in Coventry late at night. To keep warm they set light to some cardboard inside a metal skip that stands against the warehouse wall. They genuinely believe the fire will burn out safely inside the skip, and then leave. The fire spreads to the plastic cladding of the warehouse, causing £60,000 of damage. Priya is charged with arson, the prosecution alleging that she was reckless as to whether the warehouse would be damaged. The jury accept that the risk would have been obvious to an ordinary prudent adult, but also accept that the risk never crossed Priya's mind.
Which of the following best describes whether Priya was reckless as to the damage to the warehouse?

item.title: Transferred malice where the blow strikes an unintended victim
item.description:
Ryan Doyle has a long-running feud with Marcus Bell. Outside a nightclub in Newcastle, Ryan swings an iron bar at Marcus's head, intending to cause him really serious injury. Marcus ducks, and the bar strikes Leah Ward, a bystander whom Ryan had not noticed. Leah dies from a head injury. Ryan is charged with Leah's murder. He says he had no intention of harming Leah and did not know she was there.
Which of the following best describes Ryan's liability for Leah's death?

item.title: Mens rea for assault occasioning actual bodily harm (s.47 OAPA 1861; R v Savage)
item.description:
At an office party in Bristol, Hannah Price argues with her colleague Dev Mistry. Intending only to push him away from her, she shoves him hard in the chest. Dev stumbles backwards, falls against a table and suffers a cut to his head that needs stitches, which amounts to actual bodily harm. Hannah is charged under s.47 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861. She says, and the jury accept, that she neither intended nor foresaw that Dev would suffer any injury.
Which of the following best describes Hannah's liability under s.47?

item.title: Mens rea of 'maliciously' inflicting grievous bodily harm (s.20 OAPA 1861; R v Mowatt)
item.description:
In a rugby club bar in Gloucester, Callum Reid shoves Owen Price hard during an argument. Callum realises that the shove might knock Owen over and leave him bruised, but it does not occur to him that Owen could be seriously hurt. Owen falls, strikes his head on a step and suffers a fractured skull, which is grievous bodily harm. Callum is charged with inflicting grievous bodily harm contrary to s.20 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861.
Which of the following best states the mens rea the prosecution must prove under s.20?

item.title: Wounding with intent to resist lawful arrest (s.18 OAPA 1861)
item.description:
PC Amira Hussain lawfully arrests Jordan Clarke for shoplifting outside a supermarket in Reading. Determined to get away, Jordan lashes out at her with a bunch of keys held in his fist, intending to break free. He realises he may injure her but does not intend to cause her serious harm. The keys break the skin of her cheek, causing a wound. Jordan is charged under s.18 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861.
Which of the following best describes Jordan's liability under s.18?

item.title: Consent to actual bodily harm for sexual gratification (Domestic Abuse Act 2021, s.71)
item.description:
Elliot and Sam, both adults, are in a relationship and live together in Manchester. During consensual sexual activity, and at Sam's request, Elliot strikes Sam repeatedly with a leather belt for the sexual gratification of both of them. Sam is left with heavy bruising and welts that amount to actual bodily harm. Sam does not support a prosecution, but Elliot is charged with assault occasioning actual bodily harm under s.47 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861. Elliot says Sam fully consented.
Which of the following best describes whether Sam's consent provides Elliot with a defence?

item.title: Murder: an intention to cause grievous bodily harm is sufficient mens rea
item.description:
During a fight outside a pub in Wolverhampton, Kofi Mensah knocks Ahmed Raza to the ground and repeatedly kicks him in the head, intending to cause him really serious injury. Ahmed dies of a brain haemorrhage. Kofi is charged with murder. He tells police: 'I wanted to hurt him badly, but I never wanted him dead.' The jury believe him.
Which of the following best describes Kofi's liability?

item.title: Death over three years after the injury: Attorney General's consent (Year and a Day Rule Act 1996)
item.description:
On 14 January 2023, Gareth Lloyd was attacked with a knife in Swansea and left with a severe brain injury. The attacker could not then be identified. Gareth died from complications of the injury on 2 July 2026. In August 2026 DNA evidence identifies Bethany Rowe as the attacker. The Crown Prosecution Service wishes to charge her with Gareth's murder. She has never been convicted of any offence connected with the attack.
Which of the following best describes the position on bringing a murder prosecution against Bethany?

item.title: Loss of control: considered desire for revenge (Coroners and Justice Act 2009, s.54(4))
item.description:
Nadia Khan's neighbour, Graham Pike, has harassed her for months. One evening he tells her, laughing, that he has poisoned her dog, which has just died. Nadia goes home and spends two hours thinking about what he has done. She then takes a hammer from her shed, waits behind his garden wall until he returns from the pub, and kills him with several blows. She tells the police: 'I wanted him to pay for what he did.' She is charged with murder and wishes to rely on the partial defence of loss of control.
Which of the following best describes whether the partial defence of loss of control is available to Nadia?

item.title: Diminished responsibility: elements, burden and effect (Homicide Act 1957, s.2)
item.description:
Oliver Grant, who has a diagnosed severe depressive illness, kills his business partner, Simon Hale, after a dispute about the business's debts. At his trial for murder in Birmingham, two psychiatrists give evidence that his illness substantially impaired his ability to form a rational judgment and was a significant contributory factor in causing him to kill. Oliver relies on diminished responsibility.
Which of the following best describes how the defence of diminished responsibility operates in Oliver's case?

item.title: Unlawful act manslaughter: the objective dangerousness test (R v Church)
item.description:
During an argument in a pub in Hull, Leon Ford throws a heavy glass ashtray towards Femi Adeyemi, intending only to frighten him and meaning it to miss. It strikes Femi on the temple and he dies. The jury accept that Leon genuinely did not foresee that Femi might be harmed. They are sure that throwing the ashtray was an assault, and that all sober and reasonable people would have realised it carried a risk of some harm to Femi. Leon is charged with manslaughter.
Which of the following best describes Leon's liability for unlawful act manslaughter?

item.title: Gross negligence manslaughter: the risk must be of death, not serious injury (R v Rose)
item.description:
Graham Hughes, a site supervisor for a scaffolding firm in Milton Keynes, fails to make sure that a guard rail on a high platform is secured. A labourer falls from the platform and dies. Graham is tried for gross negligence manslaughter. The judge directs the jury that they may convict if they are sure that Graham owed the labourer a duty of care, that he breached it, that the breach caused the death, that a reasonably prudent person in his position would have foreseen a serious and obvious risk of serious injury, and that his negligence was so bad as to be criminal.
Which of the following best describes whether the judge's direction was correct?

item.title: Theft of money received by mistake (Theft Act 1968, s.5(4))
item.description:
Zainab Hassan's employer, a retailer in Nottingham, mistakenly pays her £1,800 more than her monthly salary by bank transfer. She notices the next day and knows it is a mistake that she should repay. She decides to keep the money and spends it on a holiday. The jury are sure that she was dishonest. She is charged with theft of the £1,800 credit balance.
Which of the following best describes whether the property 'belonged to another' for the purposes of theft?

item.title: Borrowing that is equivalent to an outright taking (Theft Act 1968, s.6(1))
item.description:
Rhys Morgan's housemate in Cambridge has an annual rail season ticket that expires on 30 June. On 1 June, without permission, Rhys takes the ticket from the housemate's desk. He uses it every day to commute, and on 1 July puts it back on the desk. He intended throughout to return it only once it had expired. He is charged with theft of the ticket and says he always meant to give it back.
Which of the following best describes whether Rhys intended permanently to deprive his housemate of the ticket?

item.title: Robbery: force must be used in order to steal (Theft Act 1968, s.8)
item.description:
Outside a takeaway in Sunderland, Dean Walsh punches Kieran Moss and knocks him to the ground because Kieran insulted Dean's football team. Kieran's phone falls out of his pocket. Only then does Dean decide to take it. He picks it up and walks off, without using or threatening any further force. He is charged with robbery.
Which of the following best describes Dean's liability for robbery?

item.title: Burglary by entering part of a building as a trespasser (Theft Act 1968, s.9(1)(a))
item.description:
Ethan Brooks goes into an electronics shop in Exeter during opening hours. He walks through a door marked 'Staff only' into the stockroom, intending to steal a games console. He is stopped by a member of staff before he picks anything up.
Which of the following best describes Ethan's liability for burglary?

item.title: Aggravated burglary: when is an article a 'weapon of offence'? (Theft Act 1968, s.10)
item.description:
At 2am Gemma Holt breaks into a house in Norwich by using a large screwdriver she has brought with her to prise open a window. She intends to steal and never intends to use the screwdriver on anyone; she uses it only on the window. She takes jewellery from a bedroom and leaves without meeting anyone. She is charged with aggravated burglary.
Which of the following best describes Gemma's liability for aggravated burglary?

item.title: Fraud by false representation is complete without any deception or gain (Fraud Act 2006, s.2)
item.description:
Kemal Arslan lists his car for sale on a website, describing it as having 'one owner from new and a full service history'. He knows both statements are false and hopes they will get him a higher price. He submits the listing through the website's automated form. The listing attracts no enquiries and he later deletes it. The jury are sure that he was dishonest. He is charged with fraud by false representation.
Which of the following best describes Kemal's liability?

item.title: Lawful excuse based on an honest belief in the owner's consent (Criminal Damage Act 1971, s.5)
item.description:
Ben Taylor's neighbour, Mrs Ali, told him some weeks ago that she wanted the rotten fence between their gardens in Sheffield 'taken down'. She meant next spring, once she had saved for a new one. Ben misunderstood and believed she wanted it removed straight away. One Saturday he pulls down the fence panels, which belong to Mrs Ali. A more careful person would have checked with her first. Ben is charged with criminal damage and says he honestly believed she had agreed.
Which of the following best describes whether Ben has a defence?

item.title: Aggravated arson of the defendant's own property (Criminal Damage Act 1971, s.1(2) and (3))
item.description:
Victor Mills owns a detached house in Derby, where he lets a room to a lodger, Kasia. In financial difficulty, he decides to set fire to the house to make an insurance claim. At 2am, knowing that Kasia is asleep upstairs and realising that the fire might endanger her life, he sets fire to the downstairs living room. Kasia wakes and escapes unhurt. The fire badly damages the house.
Which of the following best describes Victor's liability under s.1(2) and (3) of the Criminal Damage Act 1971?

item.title: Self-defence in a householder case: grossly disproportionate force (CJIA 2008, s.76(5A))
item.description:
At 1am Rahul Mehta, at home in Leicester, comes downstairs and finds an intruder, Shane, in his kitchen. Shane turns towards the back door.
