Frightened, and believing that Shane might turn on him, Rahul hits him twice with a heavy torch, breaking his arm. Rahul is charged with inflicting grievous bodily harm and relies on self-defence. It is accepted that this is a 'householder case' within s.76(8A) of the Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008.
Which of the following best describes how the jury should approach the degree of force Rahul used?

item.title: Voluntary intoxication: specific and basic intent (DPP v Majewski)
item.description:
After drinking heavily all evening in a bar in Cardiff, Tyrone Bailey smashes a glass into Will Evans's face, causing a deep cut. He is charged with wounding with intent to do grievous bodily harm under s.18 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861, with an alternative count under s.20. There is evidence that he was so drunk he may not have formed any intention to cause serious harm. His intoxication was entirely voluntary.
Which of the following best describes the relevance of Tyrone's intoxication?

item.title: Attempt where the full offence is impossible (Criminal Attempts Act 1981, s.1(2) and (3))
item.description:
Leaving a restaurant in York, Simon Clarke takes a black umbrella from the stand. He believes it belongs to another diner and intends to keep it. In fact, unknown to him, it is his own umbrella, which he had forgotten bringing. He is charged with attempted theft.
Which of the following best describes Simon's liability for attempted theft?

item.title: Accessory liability after R v Jogee: foresight is evidence of intent, not a substitute for it
item.description:
Marcus Hill and Dwayne Price agree to burgle a warehouse in Luton at night. Marcus knows that Dwayne often carries a knife and realises that Dwayne might use it to cause serious injury if they are disturbed. Marcus has told Dwayne that if anyone comes they should run, and that nobody is to be hurt. A security guard disturbs them. Dwayne stabs him, intending to cause him grievous bodily harm, and the guard dies. Marcus is charged with murder as an accessory.
Which of the following correctly states what the prosecution must prove for Marcus to be guilty of murder?

item.title: Timing of the first review of detention before charge (PACE 1984 s.40)
item.description:
Priya Nair is arrested on suspicion of burglary and arrives at a police station in England at 09:00. The custody officer authorises her detention at 09:30 so that she can be interviewed. She has not been charged, and no review has yet taken place.
By what time must the first review of Priya's detention be carried out, and by whom?

item.title: Delaying the right to have someone informed of arrest (PACE 1984 s.56)
item.description:
Tomasz Kowalski is arrested on suspicion of robbery, an indictable offence, and is detained at a police station in England. He asks for his partner to be told that he has been arrested. The custody sergeant believes that Tomasz's brother, who is suspected of taking part in the robbery but has not yet been arrested, lives with the partner and would be alerted.
Which of the following best describes whether telling Tomasz's partner may be delayed?

item.title: Who may act as appropriate adult for a juvenile (PACE Code C para 1.7 and Notes 1B, 1F)
item.description:
Kofi Mensah, aged 15, is arrested on suspicion of assaulting his father at the family home and is taken to a police station in England. His father, the alleged victim, is at the station and offers to act as appropriate adult. Kofi's mother cannot be contacted. Also present are the duty solicitor who has come to advise Kofi, a civilian detention officer employed by the police, and Kofi's 17-year-old brother.
Which of the following persons may properly act as Kofi's appropriate adult?

item.title: Defence solicitor's role in interview and when they may be excluded (Code C 6.9-6.10, Note 6D)
item.description:
Grace Adeyemi, a solicitor, attends a police station in England to represent Joel Barnes, who is being interviewed under caution on suspicion of fraud. During the interview, the officer asks Joel a long, compound question built on an assumption Joel has not accepted. Grace intervenes, challenges the way the question is put, and advises Joel not to answer it. The interviewing officer says that if she intervenes again he will exclude her from the interview.
Which of the following best describes Grace's position?

item.title: When an identification procedure must be held and which procedure comes first (Code D 3.12, 3.14)
item.description:
Mohammed Rahman is arrested on suspicion of a street robbery in England. The victim, who had never met the robber before, saw his face for about 30 seconds under a street light and tells police she is sure she could recognise him again. In interview, Mohammed denies being the robber. No identification procedure has yet been held, and it is practicable to hold one.
What should the police do next?

item.title: Inferences from failure to account for a substance: the special warning (CJPOA 1994 s.36)
item.description:
Elena Petrova is arrested next to a freshly sprayed wall and taken to a police station in England on suspicion of criminal damage. Green paint matching the graffiti is on her hands. After consulting her solicitor, she is interviewed under caution. The officer tells her he believes the paint is there because she sprayed the wall and asks her to account for it, but does not tell her what the effect of a failure to account for it would be. She answers 'no comment'. At trial she gives no evidence and relies on no fact in her defence, and the prosecution invites the court to draw an inference under s.36.
Which of the following best describes whether an inference may be drawn under s.36 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994?

item.title: Inferences from a defendant's failure to give evidence at trial (CJPOA 1994 ss.35 and 38(3))
item.description:
Daniel Okafor is tried in the Crown Court in England for unlawful wounding. At the close of the prosecution case, his counsel tells the judge that Daniel will not give evidence. There is no suggestion that his physical or mental condition makes it undesirable for him to give evidence, and his guilt is in issue.
Which of the following best describes the position?

item.title: Refusing bail where the offence was allegedly committed on bail (Bail Act 1976 Sch 1 para 2A)
item.description:
Callum Fraser, aged 34, appears before a magistrates' court in England charged with burglary of a dwelling, an either-way offence. The burglary is alleged to have been committed while he was on bail awaiting trial for an unrelated theft. The prosecution opposes bail. The court is satisfied that, if convicted, there is a real prospect that Callum will receive an immediate custodial sentence.
Which of the following best describes the court's power in relation to bail?

item.title: Prosecution appeal against a grant of bail by magistrates (Bail (Amendment) Act 1993 s.1)
item.description:
Rhys Morgan is charged with wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm, an offence punishable with imprisonment. The Crown Prosecution Service opposes bail at his first appearance before a magistrates' court in England, but the magistrates grant him conditional bail. The prosecutor wishes to challenge the decision.
Which of the following correctly describes the procedure for a prosecution appeal against the grant of bail?

item.title: Effect of indicating a guilty plea at plea before venue (MCA 1980 s.17A)
item.description:
Amira Haddad, aged 26, appears before a magistrates' court in England charged with theft from her employer, an either-way offence. The charge is read to her and the court explains the plea before venue procedure. She indicates that she would plead guilty.
What is the effect of Amira's indication?

item.title: Binding effect of a non-custodial indication of sentence (MCA 1980 ss.20 and 20A)
item.description:
Oluwaseun Bakare, aged 41, is charged with an either-way offence before a magistrates' court in England. He indicates a not guilty plea, and the court decides that the case is more suitable for summary trial. He asks for an indication of sentence, and the court indicates that a non-custodial sentence would be more likely if he were tried summarily and pleaded guilty. He then indicates that he would plead guilty. At the sentencing hearing, a differently constituted bench considers that the offence deserves a custodial sentence.
Which of the following best describes the court's position?

item.title: Sending an adult co-defendant jointly charged with a related either-way offence (CDA 1998 s.51(5))
item.description:
Jade Thompson and Lewis Park, both adults, appear together before a magistrates' court in England. Jade is charged with robbery, which is triable only on indictment. Arising from the same incident, Jade and Lewis are jointly charged with assault occasioning actual bodily harm, an either-way offence. The court sends Jade to the Crown Court for the robbery and for the related assault.
How should the court deal with Lewis?

item.title: The prosecution's initial duty of disclosure of unused material (CPIA 1996 s.3)
item.description:
Shauna Clarke is charged with robbery and pleads not guilty. Among the material gathered by the police, which the prosecution does not intend to use, is a statement from a passer-by describing the robber as having a full beard. Shauna's appearance at the time does not match that description, and the issue at trial is identification.
What must the prosecutor do with the passer-by's statement?

item.title: Defence statements in the magistrates' court: voluntary but not risk-free (CPIA 1996 ss.6 and 11)
item.description:
Natalia Wiśniewska pleads not guilty in a magistrates' court in England to a charge of common assault, a summary offence, and her trial is fixed. The prosecution has complied with its initial duty of disclosure. Natalia asks her solicitor whether she has to give a defence statement.
What is the best advice to Natalia?

item.title: The legal burden and standard of proof where the defendant claims accident (Woolmington v DPP)
item.description:
Sofia Romano is tried in the Crown Court in England for unlawful wounding. The prosecution proves that the victim was cut by a glass Sofia was holding. Sofia gives evidence that the injury was a pure accident caused when she stumbled. There is no statutory provision placing any burden on her.
How should the judge direct the jury on the burden and standard of proof?

item.title: Withdrawing poor, unsupported identification evidence from the jury (Turnbull)
item.description:
Kieran Doyle is tried in the Crown Court in England for robbery. The only evidence that he was the robber comes from a witness who glimpsed the robber's face for about two seconds, at night, in heavy rain, from about 40 metres away through a car windscreen. There is no other evidence supporting the identification. At the close of the prosecution case, defence counsel submits that there is no case to answer.
What should the judge do?

item.title: Submission of no case to answer where the issue is a witness's reliability (R v Galbraith)
item.description:
Ravi Desai is tried in the Crown Court in England for fraud by false representation. The prosecution case rests mainly on the evidence of his former business partner, which, if believed, proves every element of the offence. In cross-examination the partner admitted making an earlier statement inconsistent with his evidence and admitted that he had a financial motive to blame Ravi. At the close of the prosecution case, the defence submits that there is no case to answer.
How should the judge approach the submission?

item.title: Excluding a confession obtained by an inducement: unreliability under PACE 1984 s.76(2)(b)
item.description:
Liam O'Connor, aged 19, is interviewed at a police station in England on suspicion of burglary, having declined legal advice. During the interview the officer tells him: 'If you admit this now, you'll be home tonight and we'll forget about the other jobs.' Liam then confesses. At trial, the defence represents to the court that the confession was obtained in consequence of what the officer said. The prosecution replies that the confession is plainly true, as CCTV shows Liam near the property.
Which of the following best describes how the court must deal with the confession?

item.title: Discretion to exclude identification evidence obtained after a Code D breach (PACE 1984 s.78)
item.description:
Before holding a video identification, an officer investigating an assault in England shows the victim a single photograph of the suspect, Andre Silva, saying 'this is the man we've arrested'. The victim then picks Andre out at the video identification. At Andre's trial, the defence applies to exclude the identification evidence on the ground of the breach of Code D.
Which of the following best describes the court's power?

item.title: Admitting the statement of a witness too frightened to testify (CJA 2003 ss.114 and 116(2)(e))
item.description:
Ibrahim Sesay is tried for wounding in England. Megan Lloyd, who saw the attack, gave the police a signed witness statement identifying Ibrahim. Before trial, she receives anonymous threats against her younger brother and refuses to give oral evidence, either in person or with special measures. There is nothing to suggest that the prosecution or anyone acting for it caused her fear. The prosecution applies to read her statement as evidence of its contents, and the defence objects.
Which of the following best describes whether Megan's statement can be admitted?

item.title: Adducing a complainant's previous convictions: non-defendant bad character (CJA 2003 s.100)
item.description:
Ali Hassan is tried for assaulting Darren Hughes outside a pub in England. Ali's defence is that Darren attacked him first and he acted in self-defence. Darren has two convictions for assault occasioning actual bodily harm within the past three years, both arising from unprovoked attacks on strangers outside pubs. Ali's counsel wishes to cross-examine Darren about the convictions. The prosecution does not agree.
Which of the following best describes whether the convictions can be put to Darren?

item.title: Attack on another's character and the power to exclude (CJA 2003 s.101(1)(g) and (3))
item.description:
Nathan Clarke is tried in the Crown Court in England for possession of a controlled drug with intent to supply. When interviewed under caution, he said that the arresting officer planted the drugs on him, and at trial his counsel puts that allegation to the officer in cross-examination. The prosecution applies to adduce Nathan's two convictions for theft, recorded 14 years ago. The defence applies to exclude the convictions.
Which of the following best describes the position?

item.title: Calculating guilty plea credit after a plea at the PTPH and a lost Newton hearing
item.description:
Zara Ahmed is charged with an either-way offence. At her first appearance in the magistrates' court she indicates a not guilty plea and the case is sent to the Crown Court. At the plea and trial preparation hearing she pleads guilty, but on a basis the prosecution does not accept. The judge holds a Newton hearing and rejects her version of events. The judge decides that the sentence after a trial would have been 24 months' imprisonment, that a one-quarter reduction would have been appropriate at the stage she pleaded, and that no further decrease is warranted beyond the guideline's normal approach to a lost Newton hearing.
Applying the Sentencing Council's guilty plea guideline, what sentence should the judge impose?

item.title: Crown Court's sentencing powers on an appeal against conviction from magistrates (SCA 1981 s.48)
item.description:
Ewan Stewart is convicted of theft by a magistrates' court in England and fined. He appeals to the Crown Court against conviction only. The Crown Court dismisses the appeal and considers that the fine was unduly lenient for the offence.
Which of the following best describes the Crown Court's power over Ewan's sentence?

item.title: Compulsory referral order for a first-time youth offender pleading guilty (SA 2020 ss.84-85)
item.description:
Ryan Brennan, aged 15, appears before a youth court in England and pleads guilty to theft, an imprisonable offence. He has never been convicted of any offence. The court does not propose to impose a custodial sentence or make a hospital order, and does not consider an absolute or conditional discharge appropriate. Referral order arrangements are available in his area.
What sentence must the court impose?

item.title: Staying court proceedings brought in breach of an arbitration agreement (Arbitration Act 1996, s 9)
item.description:
Harlow Signs Ltd supplied illuminated signage to Kestrel Retail Ltd under a written contract governed by English law. Clause 18 provides that any dispute arising out of the contract shall be referred to arbitration in London. A dispute arises about the quality of the signs and Kestrel issues a claim against Harlow in the County Court for £85,000. The claim form and particulars of claim have just been served on Harlow, which wants the dispute decided by arbitration as the contract provides. There is no suggestion that clause 18 is invalid.
What is the best advice to give Harlow?

item.title: Court's power to order ADR and costs consequences of refusing to engage (CPR 3.1(2)(o), 44.2(5)(e))
item.description:
Fenwick Logistics Ltd is defending a £240,000 multi-track claim for breach of a warehousing contract brought by Orla Byrne Foods Ltd in the County Court. At the case management conference in June 2026 the claimant invites the court to direct mediation. Fenwick's managing director instructs its solicitor to oppose this, saying that Fenwick is confident of winning at trial and that, if it wins, the court will have to award it its costs whatever happens about mediation.
Which of the following best describes the position?

item.title: Sanctions against a defendant who ignores a letter before claim (PD Pre-Action Conduct, para 16)
item.description:
Amira Haddad, a sole trader, supplied bespoke shop fittings to Brightwater Interiors Ltd, which has not paid the £150,000 price. No pre-action protocol applies. In January 2026 Amira's solicitors sent Brightwater a detailed letter before claim complying with the Practice Direction - Pre-Action Conduct and enclosing key documents. Brightwater did not reply at all. Amira issued proceedings in May 2026. Brightwater defended the claim, but Amira was awarded £150,000 after a multi-track trial. The judge finds that Brightwater's failure to respond was unreasonable non-compliance with the Practice Direction.
Which of the following orders may the court make because of Brightwater's non-compliance?

item.title: Limitation period for a claim in simple contract (Limitation Act 1980, s 5)
item.description:
Tamsin Okafor runs a print studio in Bristol. Under a written contract (not a deed), Ellis Machinery Ltd agreed to deliver a new printing press to her studio on 3 May 2021, and she paid the full price in advance. The press was never delivered. Tamsin spent the next three years trying to source a replacement and only worked out the full extent of her lost profits in September 2024. She has now consulted a solicitor about suing Ellis for breach of contract.
What limitation period applies to Tamsin's claim?

item.title: Personal injury limitation for a claimant injured as a child (Limitation Act 1980, ss 11 and 28(6))
item.description:
Leo Fernandes was born on 10 March 2009. On 1 July 2024, aged 15, he was knocked off his bicycle in Leicester by a delivery van driven negligently by an employee of Swiftdrop Couriers Ltd. He suffered a fractured leg and knew immediately that he was injured and who was responsible. No claim has yet been issued on his behalf by a litigation friend. Leo has full mental capacity. His parents ask by when a claim must be started.
Ignoring the court's discretion to disapply the time limit, by when must proceedings for Leo's personal injury claim be issued?

item.title: Applicable law where both parties live in England but the accident is abroad (Rome II, art 4(2))
item.description:
Priya Raman and her friend Hannah Brooks both live in Manchester and are habitually resident in England. While on holiday in Spain, Hannah drove a hire car that she had rented from a Spanish company, with Priya as her passenger. Hannah lost control of the car through careless driving, and Priya was injured in the crash near Malaga. After returning home Priya received follow-up treatment in Manchester. She has issued a negligence claim against Hannah in the County Court in England. The parties have made no agreement about which law should apply.
Which law will the English court apply to Priya's claim in tort?

item.title: Where to start a money claim: High Court or County Court (PD 7A, para 2.1)
item.description:
Marcus Delaney, the finance director of Pennine Steel Supplies Ltd, instructs a solicitor to recover £85,000 owed by a customer for steel delivered and invoiced. The customer has raised a dispute about some of the invoices. Marcus would like the claim issued in the High Court, which he believes will put more pressure on the customer, and he says the dispute is commercially important to his company. The claim is not a personal injury claim and no enactment requires it to be issued in a particular court.
In which court should the claim be started?

item.title: Normal track for a £72,000 contract claim with a two-day trial (CPR 26.9)
item.description:
In March 2026 Calder Analytics Ltd issued a claim against one defendant, Brightline Software Ltd, for £72,000 damages for breach of a software development contract. No other remedy is sought. A defence has been filed. Both parties' directions questionnaires estimate that, if the case is managed proportionately, the trial will last two days. Each party wishes to rely on oral evidence from one IT expert. There are no other unusual features in the case.
To which track is this claim normally allocated?

item.title: Deemed service of an application notice sent by email after 4.30 pm (CPR 6.26)
item.description:
Solicitors for Ravi Shah, the claimant in a County Court claim, need to serve an application notice and supporting witness statement on the defendant, Elmfield Developments Ltd. Elmfield's solicitors have previously confirmed in writing that they will accept service of documents by email, and have given their email address. Ravi's solicitors email the documents to that address at 5.10 pm on Friday 5 June 2026. Monday 8 June 2026 is not a bank holiday.
On what date are the documents deemed to be served?

item.title: Failing to apply in time to dispute jurisdiction after acknowledging service (CPR 11(4)-(5))
item.description:
Meridian Freight Ltd was served at its London office with a claim form and particulars of claim brought by Castell Trading Ltd. Meridian believes the contract contains an exclusive jurisdiction clause in favour of the courts of New York. On Monday 2 March 2026 Meridian filed an acknowledgment of service, indicating that it intends to contest jurisdiction. It then took no further step. On 30 March 2026 its new solicitors propose to issue an application under CPR Part 11 for a declaration that the court should not exercise jurisdiction. No extension of time has been agreed or ordered.
Which of the following best describes Meridian's position under CPR Part 11?

item.title: Default judgment entered after a late defence had been filed must be set aside (CPR 12.3(2), 13.2)
item.description:
Okoro Plant Hire Ltd sued Thistle Groundworks Ltd for £64,000. Thistle filed an acknowledgment of service, so its defence was due by 16 April 2026. Thistle filed its defence at court on 20 April 2026, four days late. On 22 April 2026, Okoro's solicitors, unaware of the defence, filed a request for default judgment, and the court entered judgment in default of defence on 24 April 2026. Thistle applies to set the judgment aside. Okoro argues that the defence was late and has no real prospect of success.
How should the court deal with Thistle's application?

item.title: Costs consequences of discontinuing a claim (CPR 38.6)
item.description:
Selby Marine Ltd issued a multi-track claim against a single defendant, Whitcombe Boatyards Ltd, for £180,000. No interim injunction has been granted and no undertakings have been given. After disclosure, Selby's solicitors conclude that the claim is unlikely to succeed and, on Selby's instructions, file and serve a notice of discontinuance of the whole claim. No order about costs has been made and nothing has been agreed.
What is Selby's liability for costs, unless the court orders otherwise?

item.title: Defence that fails to deal with an allegation (CPR 16.5)
item.description:
Ashworth Fabrics Ltd's particulars of claim against Lanyon Upholstery Ltd allege that (1) the parties made a contract for the sale of fabric; (2) Ashworth delivered the fabric to Lanyon's premises on 4 March 2026; (3) the fabric matched the agreed specification; and (4) the price of £46,000 remains unpaid. Lanyon's defence admits paragraph (1). It denies paragraph (3), giving reasons and stating that the fabric was the wrong weight. It says it will put Ashworth to proof of the amount claimed in paragraph (4). The defence says nothing at all about paragraph (2) and does not set out any case on delivery.
How will the allegation in paragraph (2), about delivery on 4 March 2026, be treated?

item.title: Amending particulars of claim after service (CPR 17.1(2))
item.description:
Three weeks ago, Bramwell Events Ltd served particulars of claim on Corvin Catering Ltd claiming damages for breach of a catering contract. Corvin has not yet filed a defence. Bramwell's solicitor now realises that the particulars omit a head of loss for lost profits that Bramwell wishes to claim. Corvin's solicitors have said in writing that they will not consent to any amendment. The limitation period has not expired.
Which of the following best describes how Bramwell may amend its particulars of claim?

item.title: Approach to an interim prohibitory injunction (American Cyanamid principles)
item.description:
Nova Artisan Bakeries Ltd alleges that its former distributor, Greystone Foods Ltd, is about to launch a range of pastries using Nova's confidential recipes. Nova applies for an interim injunction restraining the launch until trial. The witness statements conflict sharply about whether the recipes were confidential and whether Greystone used them. Nova says that, if the launch goes ahead, the damage to its market share would be very hard to quantify. Greystone has not yet launched the range.
Which of the following best describes the approach the court should take to Nova's application?

item.title: Conditions for and limit on an interim payment order (CPR 25.20 and 25.23)
item.description:
Hollis Engineering Ltd claims £200,000 damages from Pryor Components Ltd for supplying defective gearboxes. Pryor's defence admits liability but disputes the amount of loss. Both parties' expert evidence suggests that Hollis is likely to recover between £120,000 and £150,000 at trial. Hollis is short of cash and applies for an interim payment of £140,000. Pryor is a solvent private company. The time for filing an acknowledgment of service has long passed.
Which of the following best describes the court's power to order an interim payment?

item.title: Failure to file a costs budget on time (CPR 3.13 and 3.14)
item.description:
Dunmore Developments Ltd is the claimant in a Part 7 multi-track claim for £400,000 damages for breach of a construction contract. The first costs and case management conference is listed for 15 July 2026. No order has been made dispensing with costs budgets or changing the time for filing them. Dunmore is legally represented, but its solicitors overlooked the deadline and did not file or exchange Dunmore's costs budget at least 21 days before the conference.
Unless the court otherwise orders, what is the consequence for Dunmore?

item.title: Conditions for pre-action disclosure (CPR 31.16)
item.description:
Kenji Watanabe's bakery in Leeds suffered a fire which he believes was caused by a commercial oven supplied and serviced by Thermacore Ltd. Kenji intends to sue Thermacore for breach of contract and negligence, but Thermacore has refused his request for copies of its service and fault records for the oven. Kenji's solicitor considers applying to the court for an order for disclosure of those records before issuing proceedings.
Which of the following must the court be satisfied of before it can order pre-action disclosure?

item.title: Litigation privilege: contemplated litigation and dominant purpose (SFO v ENRC; Three Rivers (No 6))
item.description:
A fire damaged Orion Storage Ltd's warehouse in Swindon. Two days later, Orion's operations director commissioned an independent fire investigator to identify the cause so that Orion could improve its safety procedures. At that time no one had suggested any claim and none was contemplated. Report 1 was delivered a month later. Three months after the fire, a tenant, Velasquez Textiles Ltd, sent a letter of claim alleging that Orion's negligence caused the fire. Orion's solicitors then instructed a fire engineer to report on liability so that they could advise Orion on defending the threatened claim (Report 2). Velasquez has now issued proceedings and seeks inspection of both reports.
Which of the following best describes whether the reports are protected by litigation privilege?

item.title: Failure to comply with hearsay notice requirements (Civil Evidence Act 1995, s 2(4); CPR 33.2)
item.description:
In a multi-track claim by Lindqvist Shipping Ltd against Barrow Port Services Ltd, Lindqvist served a signed witness statement of a former employee, Dariusz Nowak, on time, in accordance with the court's directions. Mr Nowak has since emigrated and will not attend trial. Lindqvist intends to rely on his statement at trial, but its solicitors never told Barrow that Mr Nowak would not be called or why. At trial, Barrow objects that the statement is inadmissible.
Which of the following best describes the position?

item.title: Putting written questions to the other side's expert (CPR 35.6)
item.description:
In a building dispute between Ferris Homes Ltd and Quayle Roofing Ltd, the court has given each party permission to rely on a surveyor. Quayle served its surveyor's report on Ferris on 2 March 2026. Ferris's solicitors want to put written questions to Quayle's surveyor to clarify some of the measurements. They also hope to put a second set of questions later, after their own expert has reviewed the answers. Quayle has not agreed to anything beyond what the rules allow, and no order has been made about questions to experts.
Which of the following correctly states the rule on Ferris's written questions to Quayle's surveyor?

item.title: When a witness summons is binding (CPR 34.5 and 34.7)
item.description:
Bethany Clarke is the claimant in a County Court claim for unpaid consultancy fees. The trial is listed to start on Monday 6 July 2026. A former colleague, Tomasz Wojcik, saw the key conversation but is reluctant to attend court voluntarily. Bethany's solicitor plans to ask the court to issue a witness summons requiring Mr Wojcik to attend the trial and give evidence.
As a general rule, what must happen for the witness summons to bind Mr Wojcik?

item.title: How to address a circuit judge in court
item.description:
Nadia Rahman, a newly qualified solicitor, is attending a two-day intermediate track trial in the County Court at Central London. The trial is listed before His Honour Judge Okafor, a circuit judge. Nadia will be making a short application at the start of the hearing on behalf of her client.
How should Nadia address the judge in court?

item.title: Claimant beats its own Part 36 offer at trial: calculating the additional amount (CPR 36.17(4)(d))
item.description:
Rosalind Achebe Interiors Ltd sued Cardew Hotels plc for unpaid design fees and damages in a multi-track claim to which no fixed costs regime applies. On 12 January 2026 the claimant made a valid Part 36 offer to accept £250,000 (inclusive of interest), with a 21-day relevant period. Cardew did not accept it, and the offer was not withdrawn or changed. After a trial in September 2026, the court gave judgment for the claimant for £300,000, calculated on the same basis as the offer. The court does not consider it unjust to apply the Part 36 consequences, and no previous order for an additional amount has been made.
What additional amount must the court award the claimant under Part 36?

item.title: Appeal from a circuit judge in the County Court: destination and permission (CPR 52.3, 52.6; PD 52A)
item.description:
After a three-day trial on the intermediate track, His Honour Judge Lister, a circuit judge sitting in the County Court at Birmingham, gave final judgment for £88,000 against Wexford Joinery Ltd. Wexford believes the judge misinterpreted a key contract term and wants to appeal. The decision was not made in insolvency, family or contempt proceedings, and it was not itself made on appeal.
Which of the following correctly states to which court the appeal lies and whether permission is required?

item.title: Taking control of goods under a County Court judgment of £5,000 or more (HCCCJO 1991, art 8)
item.description:
Gwen Morgan obtained a County Court judgment for £12,500 against Hartley Kitchens Ltd for unpaid fees for bookkeeping services. The claim did not arise under an agreement regulated by the Consumer Credit Act 1974. Hartley has not paid. Gwen's solicitor knows that Hartley owns valuable machinery at its workshop and wants enforcement agents to take control of it and sell it.
In which court may Gwen enforce the judgment by taking control of Hartley's goods?

item.title: Joint clients forming a company who then disagree on a shareholders' agreement term (Code 6.2)
item.description:
Priya Raman and Tomasz Nowak ask Fenwick Hale LLP to incorporate a private company limited by shares for their new catering business. They have agreed to be equal shareholders and the only directors. The firm agreed to act for both on the basis that they had a substantially common interest, and both gave informed consent in writing. Two weeks later, while the firm is drafting a shareholders' agreement, Priya says she wants a clause allowing her to buy Tomasz's shares at nominal value if he leaves the business within three years. Tomasz strongly opposes the clause. Each now asks the firm to negotiate the best terms for them on this point.
Which of the following best describes the firm's position under the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs?

item.title: Client instructs solicitor to withhold and delete a damaging disclosable document (Code 1.4 and 2.1)
item.description:
Hannah Adeyemi, a solicitor, acts for the claimant, Orbis Packaging Ltd, in a multi-track breach of contract claim in the County Court. The court has ordered standard disclosure under CPR Part 31. The client's managing director shows Hannah an internal email in which one of its directors admits that the goods in dispute were damaged in Orbis's own warehouse. The email falls within standard disclosure and is not privileged. The managing director instructs Hannah to leave it out of the list of documents and says he will delete it from the company's server that evening.
What should Hannah do?

item.title: Right-to-reply letter threatening a journalist with remedies unavailable in a civil claim (SLAPPs)
item.description:
Hollis Grant, a wealthy property developer, instructs Marlow Street Solicitors after a local journalist emails him under the 'right to reply' process. She plans to publish an article alleging that he concealed breaches of planning control. Mr Grant wants the firm to send her a letter, headed 'LEGAL NOTICE – NOT FOR PUBLICATION', warning that if she publishes she will face imprisonment and a large criminal fine, so that the article is dropped.
Which of the following best describes how the firm should respond to these instructions?

item.title: Sharing fees with an accountant who introduces company clients (Code 5.1)
item.description:
Cole & Bassi LLP agrees with Linwood Accountants that Linwood will introduce company clients needing share sale work, and that the firm will pay Linwood 10% of its profit costs on each matter introduced. The arrangement was agreed in a telephone call and nothing has been put in writing. Linwood has just introduced Ardent Tools Ltd, which has instructed the firm on the sale of its subsidiary. A partner asks what the SRA Code of Conduct requires.
Which of the following best describes what the Code requires in relation to this arrangement?

item.title: Updating a litigation client when the costs estimate will be substantially exceeded (Code 8.7)
item.description:
Neha Kapoor instructs a firm to bring a breach of contract claim against a former supplier. The client care letter estimated the firm's total costs to trial at £18,000. Since then the defendant has served a counterclaim and an expert has had to be instructed. The fee earner now realises that the total costs to trial are likely to be about £35,000. He decides to tell Ms Kapoor only when he sends the final bill, because the client care letter clearly described the figure as an estimate.
Which of the following best describes the fee earner's obligation?

item.title: Undertaking to pay an expert's fee when the client has not put the firm in funds (Code 1.3)
item.description:
Gareth Price, a solicitor, acts for the claimant in a professional negligence claim. He writes to a consulting engineer on the firm's letterhead: 'We undertake to pay your fee of £4,500 within 30 days of receipt of your report.' The engineer delivers the report. The client has since gone into insolvent liquidation and never put the firm in funds for the fee. Thirty days after receiving the report, Gareth tells the engineer that she should claim the fee from the client's liquidator.
Which of the following best describes Gareth's position under the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors?

item.title: PI client's complaint unresolved after eight weeks: Legal Ombudsman information (Code 8.4)
item.description:
Ruth Okonjo instructs a firm to bring a personal injury claim after a road traffic accident. On 3 March she complains in writing to the firm about delays in her case. By 5 May the complaint has not been resolved to her satisfaction. The firm is still investigating and plans to write to her once it has finished.
What must the firm now do?

item.title: Duty to cite an adverse Court of Appeal decision the opponent has missed (Code 2.7)
item.description:
Daniel Mensah, a solicitor-advocate, represents the defendant in a County Court breach of contract claim. His client's defence depends on arguing that an exclusion clause printed on a delivery note was incorporated into the contract. While preparing for trial, Daniel finds a recent Court of Appeal decision on materially indistinguishable facts which holds that such a clause was not incorporated. The claimant is a litigant in person and has not cited it. The judge has not mentioned it.
Which of the following best describes what Daniel must do?

item.title: Supervising partner's accountability for an unsupervised paralegal's work (Code 3.5)
item.description:
Sarah Whitlock, a partner in a personal injury firm, is the named supervisor of Liam, a paralegal who is not a solicitor. Sarah let Liam run a portfolio of road traffic accident claims with no file reviews and no checks on outgoing advice. Liam told one client that her claim was worth far less than it was, and she accepted a low offer on that basis. Sarah says she bears no responsibility because she did not do the work herself.
Which of the following best describes Sarah's position under the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors?

item.title: Settlement NDA that would stop a claimant reporting an assault to the police (NDA warning notice)
item.description:
A firm acts for a gym operator defending a negligence claim by a member, Ms Tasha Greene, who was injured when a weights machine collapsed. Ms Greene also alleges that a member of staff assaulted her during the incident. The parties have agreed a settlement, and both are legally represented. The client wants the settlement agreement to include a clause that Ms Greene will not disclose the circumstances of the incident to anyone, 'including the police or any regulator', on pain of repaying the settlement sum.
Which of the following best describes whether the firm may include the clause?

item.title: Letter to unrepresented debtor discouraging legal advice and imposing a 24-hour deadline (Code 1.2)
item.description:
A firm acts for a supplier claiming £9,000 unpaid under a contract from Bilal Hussain, a sole trader. Mr Hussain has no solicitor and has told the firm that he struggles to read formal English. The supplier wants the firm to send him a settlement agreement admitting liability and agreeing to pay interest at 30% a year (the contract provides for 4%). The covering letter is to say that he must sign within 24 hours and that 'there is no need to involve a lawyer, as this is a standard form'.
Which of the following best describes the firm's position?

item.title: COLP's duty to report suspected alteration of a signed witness statement (Code for Firms 9.1)
item.description:
Haverford Law LLP handles high volumes of personal injury claims. Its compliance officer for legal practice (COLP), Amina Yusuf, finds credible evidence during a file audit that an associate altered a client's witness statement after the client had signed it. The altered statement was then filed at court. The managing partner wants to wait for the outcome of an internal disciplinary hearing in three months' time before deciding whether to tell anyone outside the firm, to protect the firm's reputation.
What does the SRA Code of Conduct for Firms require of Amina?

item.title: Client wants to leave a significant gift to the solicitor drafting the will (Code 6.1)
item.description:
Edwin Thorne, aged 81, is a long-standing client of Clara Jennings, a solicitor. He asks her to prepare a new will leaving her his holiday cottage, worth about £250,000, to thank her for years of help. His estate is worth about £900,000. Clara is not related to him. She has no doubts about his capacity, but he says he does not want 'any more lawyers involved'.
How should Clara proceed?

item.title: Solicitor drafting a parent's will that leaves residue equally to the solicitor and siblings
item.description:
Jonah Feld, a solicitor, is asked by his widowed mother to prepare a new will. It will make the same main provision as her existing will, which another firm drafted: her residuary estate is to pass to her three children, including Jonah, in equal shares. There are no unusual gifts. His siblings know of their mother's wishes and agree with them. His mother has full capacity and does not want to pay another firm.
Which of the following best describes whether Jonah may draft the will without his mother first taking independent legal advice?

item.title: Deceased client's son asks for her will and instructions before probate (Code 6.3)
item.description:
Agnes Doyle has died. Her solicitors hold her will and their file of her instructions. Her executors are her two nieces. Her son, Patrick, who is not an executor, telephones the firm before probate has been granted. He asks for a copy of the will and an explanation of what his mother told the solicitor about why she left him only a small legacy.
What should the solicitor do?

item.title: Joint owners selling: one co-owner's instruction to pay all the proceeds to her (Code 3.1 and 6.2)
item.description:
A firm acts for Dev Malhotra and Fiona Grey, the registered proprietors of a flat, on its sale. They hold the beneficial interest as tenants in common in equal shares under a declaration of trust. They have recently separated. The day before completion, Fiona emails the firm instructing it to pay the whole net proceeds of sale into her sole bank account, because Dev owes her money. Dev knows nothing about this instruction.
Which of the following best describes how the firm should proceed?

item.title: Selling a house on the instructions of the owner's attorney under a registered LPA (Code 3.1)
item.description:
Iris Penhale, aged 89, has advanced dementia and lacks capacity to manage her property and affairs. Her daughter, Morwenna, is her attorney under a registered lasting power of attorney for property and financial affairs that contains no restrictions. Morwenna instructs a firm to sell her mother's house to pay care home fees. The firm has seen the registered LPA, and nothing suggests that Morwenna is acting other than in her mother's interests.
Which of the following best describes whether the firm may act on the sale?

item.title: Firm's own error in a trust matter: openness and own interest conflict (Code 6.1, 7.11)
item.description:
A firm acts for the trustees of the Ashdown family trust. Two years ago the trustees instructed the firm to invest £400,000 of trust money in line with a written investment strategy. An associate forgot, and the money has sat in a non-interest-bearing account ever since, causing the trust a significant loss. The trustees have not noticed. The supervising partner suggests either saying nothing and quietly investing the money now, or telling the trustees and asking them to sign a consent letter so that the firm can keep acting on all trust matters, including any claim arising from the error.
Which of the following best describes what the firm should do?

item.title: Commission received from an insurer on a restrictive covenant indemnity policy (Code 4.1)
item.description:
A firm acts for Leanne Choi on the sale of part of her land. The land is subject to an old restrictive covenant, and the buyer requires Ms Choi to provide a restrictive covenant indemnity insurance policy at her expense. The firm arranges the policy through a broker, and the insurer pays the firm £150 commission. The firm's client care letter says nothing about commissions.
What must the firm do with the £150 commission?

item.title: Acting for seller and buyer of a flat where terms are still to be negotiated (Code 6.2)
item.description:
Joy Baptiste wants to sell a buy-to-let flat to her long-standing tenant, Kofi Mensah. Both are existing clients of the same firm and want it to act for both of them to save costs. They have agreed a price of £240,000. They have not yet agreed who will pay for replacing a defective roof, how the tenancy deposit will be dealt with or the completion date, and they expect to negotiate these points.
Which of the following best describes whether the firm may act for both?

item.title: Acting for buyer and lender when the buyer hides a cash-back from the lender (Code 1.4, 6.2)
item.description:
A firm acts for Ollie Brennan on his purchase of a house for £300,000 and also for his mortgage lender. The lender's instructions, which the firm has accepted, require it to report any price reduction, cash-back or other incentive. Shortly before exchange, Ollie tells the solicitor that the seller has privately agreed to pay him £15,000 in cash after completion. The lender has been told only that the price is £300,000. Ollie says the solicitor must not tell the lender.
Which of the following best describes the solicitor's position?

item.title: Defending a client who has privately admitted guilt but wants to plead not guilty
item.description:
Danny Fitch is charged with stealing £2,000 from his employer's till. In a private conference he tells his solicitor that he took the money, but says he wants to plead not guilty because he thinks the CCTV evidence is poor quality.
Which of the following best describes how the solicitor may proceed?

item.title: Sentencing where the prosecution wrongly states the client has no previous convictions
item.description:
Kyle Moran pleads guilty in the magistrates' court to criminal damage. At sentencing, the prosecutor tells the bench that he has no previous convictions, because his record from another police area has not been found. Earlier, Kyle told his solicitor in confidence that he has two previous convictions for similar offences. He instructs her to tell the magistrates in mitigation that he is a man of good character.
Which of the following best describes the solicitor's position?

item.title: Co-defendants whose accounts conflict: acting for both (Code 6.2 and 6.5)
item.description:
A firm represents Leon Carter and Mason Reid, who are jointly charged with robbery. At first both deny any involvement. In a later private consultation Leon tells the firm that Mason planned the robbery and carried the knife, and that he intends to say so in his defence statement and at trial. Mason maintains a complete denial and has given the firm confidential details of his own account.
Which of the following best describes the firm's position?

item.title: Privileged advice mistakenly sent by seller's solicitor: must the buyer be told? (Code 6.4(d))
item.description:
Zainab Ali, a solicitor, acts for the buyer of a commercial unit. The seller's solicitors email her a set of replies to enquiries and mistakenly attach a letter of advice from the seller's counsel. The letter discusses a serious flooding risk that is not mentioned in the replies. Zainab realises at once that it is a privileged document that was sent to her by mistake.
Under paragraph 6.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, is Zainab obliged to tell her client what the letter says?

item.title: Paying an agency for referrals of defendants awaiting trial (Code 5.1(d))
item.description:
A criminal defence firm is approached by an agency that offers to refer defendants who have been charged and are awaiting trial in the Crown Court. The firm would pay the agency £100 for each client referred. The agency says the clients would be told about the payment and that the arrangement would be recorded in a written agreement.
May the firm enter into this arrangement?

item.title: Oral short lease at a market rent creates a legal lease (LPA 1925 s.54(2))
item.description:
Harriet owns the freehold of a lock-up shop in Leicester, England. In March 2026 she orally agreed to let the shop to Kwame for three years at the best rent reasonably obtainable, with no premium. Kwame moved in the next day and pays the agreed monthly rent. Nothing was put in writing.
Which of the following best describes the interest Kwame holds?

item.title: Contract for the sale of land must be signed by both parties (LP(MP)A 1989 s.2)
item.description:
Owen agreed to sell a field in Shropshire, England, to Priya for £85,000. Owen's solicitor prepared a single document setting out every term the parties had agreed. Owen signed it and sent it to Priya, who read it, telephoned Owen to say she was happy with it, but never signed it or any other copy. No deposit has been paid and neither party has acted on the arrangement. Owen now has a better offer and wants to withdraw.
Which of the following best describes the legal position?

item.title: Chattel or part of the land: degree and object of annexation (Elitestone v Morris)
item.description:
Gethin has exchanged contracts to sell his freehold smallholding in Herefordshire, England, to Laila. The contract says nothing about a timber cabin in the orchard. The cabin was built on site about 30 years ago from timber frame panels and feather boarding. It rests by its own weight on concrete blocks set in the ground and is not bolted down. It has been used as a holiday home, and it cannot be taken down and rebuilt elsewhere: it could be removed only by demolishing it. Before completion, Gethin tells Laila that the cabin is his personal property and that he intends to sell it separately.
Which of the following best describes whether the cabin passes to Laila on completion?

item.title: First registration: gift of unregistered land not registered within two months (LRA 2002 ss.4, 6, 7)
item.description:
In February 2026 Ifeoma, who owns an unregistered freehold house in Norwich, England, transferred it to her son Chidi as a gift by a deed of gift. Chidi did not apply to HM Land Registry for registration, and no application was made to extend the period for registration. In June 2026 Chidi asks his solicitor where the legal title now lies.
Which of the following best describes the position?

item.title: Express easement over registered land operates at law only when registered (LRA 2002 s.27)
item.description:
Sana is the registered proprietor of a freehold house in York, England. In January 2026 she granted her neighbour Tom, by deed, a right of way on foot and with vehicles over her driveway, for the benefit of Tom's registered freehold house, for ever. Tom paid £6,000 for the right. Neither party has made any application to HM Land Registry.
Which of the following best describes the status of Tom's right of way at present?

item.title: Protecting a beneficial interest under a trust of land: restriction, not notice (LRA 2002 s.33)
item.description:
Ana and her brother Femi bought a freehold flat in Leeds, England, as an investment. Ana alone is the registered proprietor, but Femi paid half the price and they agreed in writing that he owns half the beneficial interest. Femi does not live at the flat, which is let to a tenant. Femi wants to make sure that Ana cannot sell or mortgage the flat without his interest being protected.
Which entry should Femi seek on the register of Ana's title?

item.title: Actual occupation: occupier who fails to disclose her interest on inquiry (LRA 2002 Sch 3 para 2(b))
item.description:
Dev is the sole registered proprietor of a freehold house in Bath, England. His partner, Rosa, contributed half the purchase price on the understanding that she would own half the house, and she has lived there with him ever since. Nothing about her interest appears on the register. Dev agreed to sell the house to Imran. Before exchange, Imran's solicitor wrote to Rosa at the house asking whether she claimed any interest in the property; Rosa, an adult who fully understood the question, replied in writing that she did not. The sale was completed, the purchase money was paid to Dev alone, and Imran was registered as proprietor. Rosa now claims a half share binding on Imran.
Which of the following best describes Rosa's position against Imran?

item.title: Legal easement exercised within the year before a disposition overrides (LRA 2002 Sch 3 para 3)
item.description:
In 1990, when both plots were unregistered, the owner of Plot A, in Chester, England, granted the owner of Plot B by deed a perpetual right to run foul drainage through an underground pipe across Plot A. Plot A was later registered, but the easement has never been entered on its register. Waste from the house on Plot B has flowed through the pipe every day. In May 2026 Nadia bought Plot A for value and was registered as proprietor. The pipe is entirely underground, there are no manholes or other visible signs of it on Plot A, and Nadia did not know about it. She now wants to remove the pipe.
Which of the following best describes whether Nadia is bound by the drainage easement?

item.title: Rectification against a registered proprietor in possession (LRA 2002 Sch 4)
item.description:
When Caleb bought his registered freehold house in Exeter, England, in 2023, HM Land Registry mistakenly included in his title a three-metre strip of garden that belonged to his neighbour, Joan, and removed it from her title. Caleb did not know of the error, gave no misleading information, and took proper care throughout. Since moving in he has fenced the strip into his garden and used it every day. Joan has now discovered the mistake and applies to the registrar for the register to be altered to restore the strip to her title. Caleb does not consent.
Which of the following best describes how the application will be dealt with?

item.title: Unregistered land: unregistered estate contract void despite notice (LCA 1972 s.4(6))
item.description:
In 2024 Martin, who owns an unregistered freehold field in Lincolnshire, England, granted his neighbour Grace an option to purchase the field, by a written agreement complying with all formalities. Grace did not register the option as a land charge. In August 2026 Martin sold and conveyed the legal estate in the field to Ellis for its full market price. Before completion Martin had told Ellis about Grace's option. Consider the position at completion of the conveyance to Ellis.
Which of the following best describes whether Grace can enforce her option against Ellis?

item.title: Severance by written notice, then survivorship (LPA 1925 ss.36(2), 196(3))
item.description:
Asha, Ben and Carys bought a freehold house in Bristol, England, together as an investment. They are the registered proprietors and the transfer declares that they hold the house on trust for themselves as beneficial joint tenants. Ben and Carys live in the house; Asha lives elsewhere. On 1 September 2026 Asha signed a written notice addressed to Ben and Carys stating that she wished to sever the beneficial joint tenancy, and she pushed it through the letterbox of the house. Carys read it that evening. Ben died suddenly on 3 September 2026 without having read it. Ben left a will giving everything to his sister.
Which of the following best describes who now holds the legal title and the beneficial interests in the house?

item.title: Order for sale between co-owners: TOLATA 1996 ss.14 and 15 factors
item.description:
Erin and Joel, an unmarried couple, bought a freehold house in Reading, England, as their family home, in their joint names on trust for themselves as tenants in common in equal shares. They have a daughter aged eight. Their relationship has ended. Joel has moved out and applies to the court for an order that the house be sold. Erin and their daughter still live there, and Erin opposes a sale until their daughter finishes school.
Which of the following best describes how the court will decide Joel's application?

item.title: Trustee in bankruptcy's application for sale of the family home after one year (IA 1986 s.335A)
item.description:
Gareth and Lowri, a married couple, own their family home in Swindon, England, as beneficial joint tenants. Gareth was made bankrupt, and his estate vested in his trustee in bankruptcy in January 2025. In August 2026 the trustee applied under s.14 of the Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996 for an order for sale. Lowri, who was not responsible for the bankruptcy, lives in the house with their two children, aged 13 and 15. A sale would cause the family the disruption and hardship that a sale usually causes, but there is nothing unusual about their circumstances.
Which of the following best describes how the court will approach the application?

item.title: Lease or licence: exclusive possession for a term at a rent (Street v Mountford)
item.description:
Marco owns a row of lock-up workshops in Coventry, England. He let one unit to Siobhan, a furniture restorer, under a written document headed 'Licence Agreement'. It gives Siobhan sole use of the unit from month to month for a monthly 'licence fee', and says expressly that the parties do not intend to create a tenancy. Marco provides no services, keeps no key and has reserved only a right to enter on notice to inspect and carry out repairs. No other person uses the unit.
Which of the following best describes Siobhan's legal position?

item.title: Certainty of term: letting 'until the land is needed' to a company (Berrisford v Mexfield)
item.description:
In 2024 a district council let a yard in Stoke-on-Trent, England, to Kestrel Storage Ltd, a company, by an agreement stating that the letting would last 'until the council requires the land for the extension of its depot'. Kestrel took exclusive possession and has paid rent monthly ever since, as the agreement required. The council has no present plans to extend the depot.
Which of the following best describes the legal effect of the agreement?

item.title: Post-1995 lease: original tenant released on assignment (LT(C)A 1995 s.5)
item.description:
In 2015 Hollis Estates Ltd granted Bea a 15-year lease of a shop in Derby, England. In 2022, with Hollis's written consent as the lease required, Bea assigned the whole lease to Darius. Hollis did not ask Bea to enter into an authorised guarantee agreement, and she did not give one. Darius has now failed to pay two quarters' rent and has disappeared. Hollis asks whether it can recover the arrears from Bea.
Which of the following best describes Bea's liability?

item.title: Forfeiture for breach of a covenant other than rent: section 146 notice first (LPA 1925 s.146)
item.description:
Rhiannon is the tenant of a shop in Gloucester, England, under a ten-year commercial lease that contains a covenant against structural alterations without consent and a forfeiture clause allowing the landlord to re-enter for breach of any tenant covenant. Without asking, Rhiannon has removed an internal load-bearing wall. The landlord, Fairway Properties Ltd, wants to forfeit the lease. Rent is fully paid.
What must Fairway do before it can enforce the right of re-entry?

item.title: Easements: the right must accommodate the dominant land (Re Ellenborough Park)
item.description:
Nell owns a freehold café beside a lake in Cumbria, England. The adjoining landowner, Victor, who owns the lake, has offered to grant Nell and her successors a number of rights by deed. Nell wants to know which proposed rights would be capable of existing as easements benefiting the café land.
Which of the following proposed rights is LEAST likely to be capable of existing as an easement?

item.title: Section 62 LPA 1925: a tenant's permissive right becomes an easement on sale of the freehold
item.description:
Hugo owns a cottage and the neighbouring paddock in Dorset, England, both registered under one title. In 2019 he let the cottage to Lena on a periodic tenancy. The cottage has its own frontage to a lane, but Hugo told Lena informally that she could also drive across the paddock along a gravel track to reach the main road, and she has done so most days since. In 2026 Hugo sold and transferred the freehold of the cottage to Lena, keeping the paddock. The transfer says nothing about the track and does not exclude s.62 of the Law of Property Act 1925. Hugo now wants to stop Lena using the track.
Which of the following best describes Lena's position?

item.title: Implied easement under the rule in Wheeldon v Burrows on a sale of part
item.description:
Freya owned two adjoining plots in Suffolk, England: Plot 1, with a house and a garage at the rear, and Plot 2, a paddock. Plot 1 has a pedestrian gate onto the street at the front but no vehicle access except along a surfaced driveway across Plot 2, which Freya laid out and used daily to drive to the garage. In 2026 Freya sold Plot 1 to Gus, keeping Plot 2. The transfer says nothing about the driveway. Freya now wants to stop Gus using it.
Which of the following best describes whether Gus has a right to use the driveway?

item.title: Burden of a restrictive freehold covenant runs in equity (Tulk v Moxhay)
item.description:
In 2005 Ruth sold part of her garden in Winchester, England, to Callum. In the transfer Callum covenanted, for himself and his successors in title, with Ruth for the benefit of her retained house, not to build more than one dwelling on the plot. The covenant was protected by a notice on the register of Callum's title. In 2025 Callum sold the plot to Brightside Homes Ltd, which now plans to build three houses. Ruth still owns and lives in her retained house.
Which of the following best describes whether Ruth can enforce the covenant against Brightside?

item.title: Purchaser from a mortgagee protected despite irregular exercise of power of sale (LPA s.104(2))
item.description:
Kezia mortgaged her freehold warehouse in Bradford, England, to Northvale Bank plc by a legal charge. The legal date for redemption has passed, so the statutory power of sale has arisen, and the charge does not vary the statutory conditions on its exercise. When Kezia's interest payments were only one month in arrears, and without serving any notice requiring payment, Northvale sold the warehouse at full market value to Omar, who acted in good faith and knew nothing of the circumstances of the default. Kezia now wants the sale to Omar set aside.
Which of the following best describes the position?

item.title: Mortgagee's duty on sale: timing is for the mortgagee; true market value at sale (Silven)
item.description:
Fenwick Lending Ltd holds a first legal charge over a block of commercial units in Middlesbrough, England, owned by Tanaka Developments Ltd, which has defaulted. Fenwick's power of sale has become exercisable. The local market is depressed, and Tanaka asks Fenwick to wait a year, when prices are expected to recover, and in the meantime to apply for planning permission for residential conversion, which would increase the value. Fenwick refuses, properly markets the units and sells them at the best price reasonably obtainable at that time.
Which of the following best describes Fenwick's liability to Tanaka?

item.title: Court's power to adjourn or suspend mortgage possession of a dwelling-house (AJA 1970 s.36)
item.description:
Yusuf has a repayment mortgage of his house in Luton, England, with Clearwater Building Society. After losing his job he fell into arrears, and Clearwater has issued a claim for possession. Yusuf has now started a new, better-paid job, and the evidence shows that he can pay the normal monthly instalments plus an extra amount that would clear the arrears within two years.
Which of the following best describes the court's powers at the possession hearing?

item.title: Priority of registered charges: the order shown on the register (LRA 2002 s.48)
item.description:
Liam is the registered proprietor of a freehold house in Hull, England. On 1 March 2026 he granted a legal charge to Ashby Bank plc, and on 5 March 2026 he granted a second legal charge to Bridgeway Finance Ltd. Bridgeway applied to register its charge on 10 March and was registered. Ashby applied to register its charge on 20 March and was registered. Neither lender had the protection of a priority period under an official search, and neither charge contains any provision about priority. Liam has defaulted on both loans.
Which of the following best describes the priority of the two charges?

item.title: Conflict between SRA Principles: the wider public interest prevails over the client's interests
item.description:
Ifeoma Chukwu is a solicitor in an SRA-authorised firm in England and Wales, acting for a defendant in a county court claim. At a hearing next week her client wants her to tell the district judge that he was abroad on the date of an alleged meeting. The client has already admitted to Ifeoma, in a privileged conversation, that he was in London that day and attended the meeting. He says that acting in his best interests means saying whatever helps him win.
Which of the following best states how Ifeoma must resolve the tension between the SRA Principles in this situation?

item.title: Reserved instrument activities: Land Registry transfer v wills and powers of attorney (LSA Sch 2)
item.description:
Gareth Pryce runs Pryce Property Paperwork, a business in England that is not authorised by any approved regulator; neither Gareth nor any of his staff is an authorised or exempt person. For a fee, he offers clients five documents: (1) a lasting power of attorney; (2) a transfer (form TR1) of a registered freehold house from a seller to a buyer; (3) a will; (4) a stock transfer form for shares in a private company, containing no trust or limitation; and (5) a written agreement for decorating services that is not intended to be executed as a deed.
Which document can Gareth's business NOT lawfully prepare for a fee, because preparing it is a reserved legal activity?

item.title: Admitting a non-lawyer member to a law firm LLP makes it a licensable body (LSA 2007 s.72)
item.description:
Hollins Quarrie LLP is an SRA-authorised firm in England whose members are all solicitors. The members want to admit Priya Raman, a chartered accountant who is not an authorised person under the Legal Services Act 2007, as a member of the LLP with a 5% share of the profits and voting rights, so that she can run the firm's finances. The firm will continue to carry on reserved legal activities.
What is the regulatory consequence of admitting Priya as a member of the LLP?

item.title: Closing a firm with no successor: six years' run-off cover under the SRA Minimum Terms
item.description:
Delroy Campbell is a sole practitioner whose SRA-authorised firm in England has qualifying professional indemnity insurance on the SRA Minimum Terms and Conditions (MTC). He retires and closes the practice at the end of the policy period. No other firm takes over the practice, so there is no successor practice. Two years later a former client, Martina Kovač, discovers that Delroy made a negligent mistake in her property transaction shortly before he retired.
Which of the following best describes the indemnity insurance position for Martina's claim?

item.title: SRA Transparency Rules: which advertised service requires published cost information?
item.description:
Ashworth & Bello is an SRA-authorised firm in Manchester. Its website advertises the following services to individual clients, none of them publicly funded: (1) administering the estates of people who have died, where the assets are all in the UK and nothing is contested; (2) personal injury claims; (3) asylum appeals in the First-tier Tribunal; (4) defending serious charges in the Crown Court; and (5) bringing claims for contested wills and disputed inheritances.
For which advertised service must the firm publish cost information on its website under the SRA Transparency Rules?

item.title: Equality Act 2010: no charging a disabled client for a reasonable adjustment (s.20(7))
item.description:
Tomasz Wiśniewski, who is profoundly deaf and uses British Sign Language, instructs Lowther Grange, an SRA-authorised firm in Leeds, on a dispute with his landlord. The firm accepts that providing a BSL interpreter at his meetings with his solicitor is a reasonable step to avoid the substantial disadvantage he would otherwise face. The supervising partner suggests adding the interpreter's fees to Tomasz's bill as a disbursement, explaining this in the client care letter.
What is the correct position on the interpreter's fees?

item.title: Savings built up from tax evasion are criminal property (POCA 2002 s.340)
item.description:
Rhiannon Lewis instructs Calder Vane, an SRA-authorised firm in Cardiff, to act on her purchase of a flat for cash. While discussing source of funds, she tells the conveyancing solicitor that the purchase money is savings from her catering business, which has always been run legitimately, but that for several years she deliberately left a large part of her takings off her tax returns 'like everyone does', so she has paid far less income tax than she owed. The money has been held in her ordinary savings account throughout.
Which of the following best describes the status of the savings under Part 7 of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002?

item.title: Conducting and settling litigation is not a s.328 POCA arrangement (Bowman v Fels)
item.description:
Mehmet Arslan, a solicitor, acts for Daniela Ferreira in county court proceedings in England against her former business partner, Carl Royston, for her share of the proceeds of a property they jointly developed. Documents disclosed by Carl in the proceedings lead Mehmet to suspect that Carl under-declared VAT on the development, so that part of the money Carl will use to satisfy any judgment or settlement may be criminal property. Carl's solicitors now propose a settlement that, in Mehmet's view, genuinely reflects the merits of Daniela's claim. Daniela wants to accept it.
Which of the following best describes Mehmet's position under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002?

item.title: Failure to disclose (POCA s.330): no privilege for information given to further a crime
item.description:
Joanna Mazur, a solicitor at an SRA-authorised firm in Bristol, is acting for Kofi Mensah on his purchase of a house, a matter within the regulated sector. In a meeting at which she is advising him on the purchase, Kofi tells her that the deposit and the balance of the price will come from cash his brother made selling stolen goods, and asks her to complete quickly so the money is 'turned into bricks' before anyone asks questions. Joanna is the firm's fee-earner, not its nominated officer.
What is Joanna's obligation under s.330 of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002?

item.title: Tipping off: telling a client of a report to dissuade an offence (POCA ss.333A and 333D(2))
item.description:
The money laundering reporting officer of Penrose Achebe LLP, an SRA-authorised firm in Birmingham, has made a suspicious activity report to the National Crime Agency about funds a client, Lukas Becker, wanted to use to buy shares in a private company. The firm did not proceed. A week later Lukas tells his solicitor, Grace Penrose, that he plans to put the same funds through a different purchase. Grace tells him: 'We have had to report our concerns about where this money came from. If you go ahead with this, you will be committing an offence.' She says this solely to persuade him not to go ahead.
Has Grace committed the offence of tipping off under s.333A of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002?

item.title: Deemed consent after a DAML: the seven working day notice period (POCA s.335)
item.description:
Hartfield Oduya, an SRA-authorised firm in London, acts for a seller of commercial property. The firm's nominated officer suspects that part of the buyer's funds may be criminal property. On Tuesday 3 March 2026 she makes an authorised disclosure to the National Crime Agency seeking consent for the firm to complete the sale. None of the days that follow is a bank holiday. The firm hears nothing at all from the NCA.
Assuming the NCA does not give notice refusing consent, from which date may the firm first treat itself as having the appropriate consent to complete?

item.title: Domestic politically exposed persons: enhanced due diligence still required (MLR 2017 reg 35)
item.description:
Sandeep Gill, a serving member of the House of Commons, asks Wexley Thorne LLP, an SRA-authorised firm in England, to act on his purchase of a house in London for £1.2 million. The firm's risk-management systems identify him as a politically exposed person. Having assessed the risk, the firm finds no enhanced risk factors beyond his status as a domestic PEP and decides it is willing to act.
Under the Money Laundering Regulations 2017, what must the firm do in addition to its standard customer due diligence before establishing the business relationship?

item.title: Beneficial owners of a company client: individuals holding more than 25% (MLR 2017 reg 5)
item.description:
Brightwater Interiors Ltd, an unlisted company, instructs Fenwick Adeyemi, an SRA-authorised firm in England, to act on its purchase of a warehouse. The company's shares and voting rights are held by four individuals: Helena Novak 30%, Marcus Obi 25%, Saoirse Kelly 25% and Daniel Price 20%. Each holds directly, and no one exercises control over the company's management in any other way.
Which individual or individuals are beneficial owners of the company under the Money Laundering Regulations 2017?

item.title: Breach of the general prohibition: agreement unenforceable against the client (FSMA s.26)
item.description:
Corrigan Mbeki, an SRA-authorised firm in England that is not authorised by the FCA, agreed with a client, Elena Petrova, to arrange her purchase of a portfolio of listed shares as a stand-alone service for a fee of £4,000, unconnected with any other legal work for her. The arrangement did not fall within any exclusion, and the firm could not rely on the exemption for professional firms in Part 20 of FSMA because the service was not incidental to legal services. Elena has paid £2,000 and refuses to pay the balance.
Which of the following best describes the civil consequences of the agreement with Elena?

item.title: Recognising a specified investment: company shares v land and goods (RAO art 76)
item.description:
Monique Delacroix is the executor of her late father's estate in England and has instructed Ravensworth Hale, an SRA-authorised firm, to help administer it. The estate includes: a freehold house in Kent; a classic car; a painting by a minor Victorian artist; a long leasehold flat in Brighton; and 2,000 ordinary shares in a company listed on the London Stock Exchange. Monique asks which of these assets could bring the firm's work within the financial services regime if the firm arranged its sale.
Which asset is a specified investment for the purposes of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000?

item.title: Introducing a client to an independent financial adviser: the introducing exclusion (RAO art 33)
item.description:
Wilhelmina Asante has inherited £300,000 and asks her solicitor, Rupert Hale of an SRA-authorised firm in York that is not FCA-authorised, what she should invest in. Rupert gives no view on any investment. Instead he refers her to Okafor Wealth, an independent financial adviser authorised by the FCA, so that it can give her independent advice on investments generally. Rupert's firm receives no fee or commission for the introduction. The introduction is not made with a view to any transaction relating to a contract of insurance.
Which of the following best describes whether Rupert's introduction is a regulated activity?

item.title: Commission and the Part 20 exemption: accounting to the client (FSMA 2000 s.327(3))
item.description:
Ainsley Brook, an SRA-authorised firm in England that is not authorised by the FCA, is administering an estate. As an incidental part of that work, and relying on the exemption in Part 20 of FSMA 2000, the firm arranges for the executors to sell the deceased's holding of listed shares through an FCA-authorised stockbroker. The stockbroker pays Ainsley Brook a commission of £1,150 for the business. The firm's practice manager suggests keeping the commission as general firm income.
What must the firm do with the commission if it is to continue to rely on the exemption for professional firms?

item.title: SRA Financial Services (Scope) Rules: acting as nominated adviser on an AIM admission is prohibited
item.description:
Kingsley Ruiz LLP is an SRA-authorised firm in London that is not authorised by the FCA. Its corporate department acts for Tidemark Robotics plc, which is seeking admission of its shares to the Alternative Investment Market (AIM) of the London Stock Exchange. The board asks the firm to take on several roles in the transaction.
Which role is Kingsley Ruiz LLP prohibited from taking by the SRA Financial Services (Scope) Rules?

item.title: Personal injury CFA: success fee capped at 25% of damages excluding future loss (2013 Order)
item.description:
