Nadia Rahman instructed Pennington Lowe, an SRA-authorised firm in England, under a conditional fee agreement entered into in 2025 for her personal injury claim arising from an accident at work. The agreement provides for a success fee of 100% of base costs and caps it in accordance with the Conditional Fee Agreements Order 2013. The claim settles at first instance for: general damages for pain, suffering and loss of amenity £40,000; past loss of earnings £12,000; and future loss of earnings £80,000. Nothing is recoverable by the Compensation Recovery Unit. The firm's base costs are £30,000. Ignore VAT.
What is the maximum success fee the firm may charge Nadia?

item.title: CFA success fees are not recoverable from the losing opponent (CLSA 1990 s.58A(6))
item.description:
Callum Fraser is considering bringing a High Court claim in England for breach of contract against a former supplier. His solicitor proposes a conditional fee agreement with a success fee of 50% of base costs, entered into now. Callum asks: 'If I win and the court orders the supplier to pay my costs, will the supplier also have to pay your success fee?'
Which of the following is the correct answer to Callum's question?

item.title: Damages-based agreements in employment claims: the 35% cap including VAT (DBA Regs reg 7)
item.description:
Aisha Bello brings an unfair dismissal and discrimination claim in the employment tribunal in England. She instructs Marlow Achterberg, an SRA-authorised firm, under a damages-based agreement made in 2025. The tribunal awards her £60,000, all of which she recovers from her former employer. The agreement provides for the firm's payment to be the maximum percentage of her recovery permitted by law.
What is the maximum payment the firm may receive from Aisha under the damages-based agreement?

item.title: Civil legal aid scope: possession of the client's home v excluded services (LASPO Sch 1)
item.description:
Five people visit a legal aid drop-in clinic run by an SRA-authorised firm in Sheffield. Each would meet the financial eligibility and merits criteria if their matter is within scope. Jade wants to sue a supermarket after slipping and breaking her wrist. Rashid wants to defend a possession claim his landlord has issued against his home. Ewa wants to sue a neighbour for defamation. Thomas wants advice on a dispute about a family trust. Precious wants to sue a neighbour for trespass to land over a disputed boundary.
Whose matter is within the scope of civil legal aid under Part 1 of Schedule 1 to the Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders Act 2012?

item.title: Legal expenses insurance: checking for before-the-event cover at the outset (Sarwar v Alam)
item.description:
Oluwaseun Adebayo was injured when a car hit him while he was cycling in Nottingham. He consults Harrow Penney, an SRA-authorised firm, about a claim against the driver which he values at around £25,000. At the first meeting, the solicitor discusses how the claim might be funded.
Which step best reflects proper practice for the solicitor when considering funding at the outset?

item.title: Acting for both seller and buyer of a residential property (SRA Code of Conduct, para 6.2)
item.description:
Nkechi Obi, a solicitor in England, acts for Martin Haldane on the sale of his house in Reading. Martin has agreed a price of £465,000 with Sunita Varma, a first-time buyer he met through an estate agent; they are not related and have never met before. Sunita asks Nkechi to act for her on the purchase as well, saying it would save time and money. Both Martin and Sunita are willing to sign a written consent to Nkechi acting for both of them.
Which of the following best describes whether Nkechi may act for Sunita as well as Martin?

item.title: Form A restriction and a sale by a surviving co-owner (registered title)
item.description:
You act for Callum Reid, who is buying a registered freehold house in Bristol for £390,000. The official copies show Joan Petrie and Helen Okafor as registered proprietors, and the proprietorship register contains the standard Form A restriction: "No disposition by a sole proprietor of the registered estate (except a trust corporation) under which capital money arises is to be registered unless authorised by an order of the court." Helen died last year. Joan is selling the house and has produced Helen's death certificate. Helen's will appoints her son, Daniel Okafor, as executor; he has not been appointed a trustee of the legal estate. Joan does not claim to have become solely beneficially entitled.
What should Callum's solicitor require in order to obtain good title and register the transfer?

item.title: Length of title an unregistered seller must deduce (LPA 1969, s.23)
item.description:
Grace Adeyemi is selling a freehold cottage in rural Herefordshire. The title is unregistered: assume the land was not in an area of compulsory registration at the time of either conveyance. Her title deeds include a conveyance on sale dated 1974 from Arthur Bell to Ivor Pugh, and a conveyance on sale dated 1988 from Ivor Pugh to Grace. There have been no dealings since 1988. The draft contract says nothing about the root of title or the length of title to be deduced. The buyer's solicitor insists on seeing the 1974 conveyance as well.
Which of the following best describes the title Grace must deduce?

item.title: Planning enforcement time limit for unauthorised building works in England (TCPA 1990, s.171B)
item.description:
In October 2026 you act for Leila Haddad on her proposed purchase of a semi-detached house in Leicester, England. Replies to enquiries reveal that the seller built a large two-storey rear extension without planning permission. Building work was substantially completed in March 2025. The local planning authority has taken no action so far. Leila asks whether the extension is now safe from planning enforcement.
Which of the following best describes the position on planning enforcement?

item.title: Change of use within Use Class E is not development (TCPA 1990, s.55(2)(f))
item.description:
Marek Nowak is buying the freehold of a lock-up shop in Norwich, England, which has been used for the retail sale of clothing. He plans to turn it into a café where customers will mostly eat and drink on the premises. He will make only internal changes (new counters and seating) that will not affect the external appearance of the building. There are no planning conditions or other restrictions on use affecting the shop.
Does Marek need planning permission for the change from clothes shop to café?

item.title: Using the buyer's deposit on the seller's related purchase (SCS 5th ed, condition 2.2.5)
item.description:
You act for Priya Raman on the sale of her flat in Sheffield for £320,000. The contract incorporates the Standard Conditions of Sale (Fifth Edition, 2018 Revision) without amendment, and the buyer will pay a 10% deposit of £32,000 on exchange. Priya is buying a house in Harrogate, England, to live in, and the two transactions will be exchanged on the same day. She has £10,000 of her own savings available and asks whether the £32,000 can be used towards the 10% deposit of £40,000 on her purchase.
Which of the following best describes the position under the Standard Conditions of Sale?

item.title: Risk of damage between exchange and completion (SCS 5th ed, condition 5.1.1)
item.description:
Tomasz Kowalski exchanged contracts to buy a detached house in Exeter for £410,000. The contract incorporates the Standard Conditions of Sale (Fifth Edition, 2018 Revision) without amendment, and no special condition deals with insurance. The seller's buildings insurance is not required by the contract to continue. Tomasz did not arrange his own buildings insurance, intending to do so from completion. A week before completion, a fire caused by a lightning strike seriously damaged the house.
Which of the following best describes Tomasz's position?

item.title: Calculating contractual compensation for late completion (SCS 5th ed, condition 7.2)
item.description:
Ola Bankole sold a house in Northampton to Ben Ashworth for £400,000. The contract incorporates the Standard Conditions of Sale (Fifth Edition, 2018 Revision) and a special condition providing that the contract rate is 8% per annum. Ben paid a deposit of £40,000 on exchange. Completion was delayed and took place 10 days after the contractual completion date. It is agreed that Ben's total period of default was 10 days and that Ola's total period of default (a delay in providing a document she was obliged to supply) was 3 days. Assume a 365-day year.
How much compensation, if any, is payable under condition 7.2, and by whom?

item.title: Execution of a transfer deed by a company with a sole director (Companies Act 2006, s.44)
item.description:
Kestrel Lane Developments Ltd, a private company, is selling a registered freehold plot in Swindon. It has one director, Farida Mensah, and no company secretary, and it has no common seal. The buyer's solicitor has sent the TR1 transfer for execution by the company as a deed.
How may the transfer be validly executed by the company?

item.title: Failure to apply for first registration within two months (LRA 2002, ss.6 and 7)
item.description:
On 2 March 2026 Ifeoma Chukwu completed her purchase of an unregistered freehold house in Shropshire from Gerald Watts, under a conveyance on sale. Her solicitor's firm overlooked the application for first registration. The mistake is discovered on 18 May 2026, and no order extending the registration period has been made.
Which of the following best describes the current position?

item.title: SDLT on a residential purchase above the first-time buyers' relief limit
item.description:
Amara Eze and Jonah Fisher, who have never owned a home anywhere, complete the purchase of a freehold house in Brighton, England, on 3 July 2026 for £520,000, to live in as their only residence. Assume the following SDLT rates and relief apply. Standard residential rates: 0% on the first £125,000; 2% on the portion from £125,001 to £250,000; 5% on the portion from £250,001 to £925,000; 10% on the portion from £925,001 to £1.5 million; 12% above £1.5 million. First-time buyers' relief: 0% up to £300,000 and 5% on the portion from £300,001 to £500,000, but the relief cannot be claimed if the price is over £500,000.
How much SDLT is payable?

item.title: Deadline for the SDLT return and payment after completion (FA 2003, ss.76 and 86)
item.description:
You act for Rhys Morgan, who exchanged contracts on 19 June 2026 and completed on 3 July 2026 the purchase of a freehold house in Kent, England, for £360,000 with the help of a mortgage. SDLT is payable. Rhys did not take possession before completion.
What must be done about SDLT, and by when?

item.title: Land Transaction Tax return for a purchase in Wales (LTTA 2017, s.44)
item.description:
Seren Evans, a solicitor in Chester, England, acts for Dafydd Lloyd on his purchase of a freehold shop in Cardiff for £600,000. Completion takes place on 10 July 2026. Dafydd did not take possession before completion. Seren has previously handled only purchases of land in England.
Which of the following best describes what must be done after completion to deal with tax on the purchase?

item.title: Landlord's statutory duties on an application for consent to assign (LTA 1988, ss.1 and 4)
item.description:
Bluewater Coffee Ltd holds a ten-year lease of a café in Bath. The lease contains a covenant not to assign the whole without the landlord's consent, such consent not to be unreasonably withheld. On 1 June 2026 Bluewater sent the landlord, Halcyon Estates Ltd, a written application for consent to assign to a well-established restaurant chain, with full references and accounts. Halcyon did not respond for ten weeks and then told Bluewater by telephone that consent was refused, without giving any reasons. Meanwhile the proposed assignee withdrew.
Which of the following best describes Bluewater's position?

item.title: Pre-agreed AGA condition in a post-1995 commercial lease (LTA 1927, s.19(1A))
item.description:
In 2021 Fenwick Properties Ltd granted Orla Byrne Design Ltd a 15-year lease of offices in Manchester. The lease contains a covenant not to assign without the landlord's consent, such consent not to be unreasonably withheld. It also states, for the purposes of s.19(1A) of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1927, that the landlord may require, as a condition of consent to any assignment, that the assigning tenant enters into an authorised guarantee agreement (AGA). Orla Byrne Design now wishes to assign to a large, financially strong company. Fenwick agrees to consent on condition that Orla Byrne Design enters into an AGA. Orla Byrne Design argues that the condition is unreasonable because the assignee's covenant is stronger than its own.
Which of the following best describes whether Fenwick may impose the AGA condition?

item.title: Cap on damages for breach of a tenant's repairing covenant (LTA 1927, s.18(1))
item.description:
Thornbury Logistics Ltd held a 12-year lease of a warehouse in Leeds, which expired on 30 June 2026. The lease contained a covenant to keep the premises in good repair and to yield them up in that condition at the end of the term. Thornbury left the roof and cladding in disrepair. The landlord's surveyor puts the cost of the remedial works at £120,000. A valuer reports that the disrepair has reduced the value of the landlord's reversion by £70,000. The landlord intends to re-let the warehouse in its existing form and has no plans to demolish or alter it.
What is the maximum the landlord can recover as damages for breach of the repairing covenant?

item.title: Contracting out of LTA 1954 security of tenure when the warning notice is served late (s.38A)
item.description:
Zainab Hussain is taking a five-year lease of a small office in Leicester for her accountancy practice. The parties have agreed that the lease will be contracted out of the security of tenure provisions of Part II of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954. Completion of the lease is fixed for 15 July 2026, and Zainab will not be contractually bound before then. The landlord's solicitor serves the prescribed warning notice on Zainab on 9 July 2026, six days before completion.
What must happen for the contracting-out agreement to be valid?

item.title: Landlord's response to a tenant's section 26 request (LTA 1954, s.26)
item.description:
Pemberton Print Ltd holds a ten-year lease of a print works in Coventry, expiring on 31 March 2027. The lease is not contracted out, and Pemberton occupies the premises for its business. On 6 July 2026 Pemberton's solicitor gave the landlord, Ashgrove Holdings Ltd, a valid request for a new tenancy under s.26 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954, proposing a new tenancy beginning on 31 March 2027. Ashgrove has not served any notice under s.25. It wants to oppose renewal on the ground that it intends to occupy the premises for its own business (ground (g)).
What must Ashgrove do to preserve its right to oppose a new tenancy?

item.title: Statutory compensation when renewal is refused on ground (f) only (LTA 1954, s.37)
item.description:
Nadia Rahman has run her bookshop in York from the same premises since 2009, first under a 2009 lease and then under a renewal lease granted in 2019, which is not contracted out. Her landlord served a s.25 notice opposing a new tenancy on grounds (b) (persistent delay in paying rent) and (f) (intention to demolish or reconstruct). Nadia applied to court for a new tenancy. The court rejected ground (b), finding the rent arrears trivial, but upheld ground (f) and refused a new tenancy. The rateable value of the holding is £36,000. Assume the appropriate multiplier is 1 and the lease does not exclude compensation.
What compensation, if any, is Nadia entitled to on quitting the holding?

item.title: VAT on the sale of an opted commercial building under the SCPC (condition 2)
item.description:
Corvid Investments Ltd is selling a vacant freehold office building in Birmingham, built in 2005, for £2,000,000. Several years ago Corvid exercised an option to tax the building. The buyer is Harbour Mutual Insurance plc, an insurer whose supplies are almost all exempt from VAT. The contract incorporates the Standard Commercial Property Conditions (Third Edition, 2018 Revision). None of the Part 2 conditions is incorporated, and there is no special condition about VAT.
Which of the following best describes the VAT position under the contract?

item.title: Private residence relief on a former home later let (TCGA 1992, s.223)
item.description:
On 1 January 2012 Kemi Adebayo bought a flat in Bristol, which she occupied as her only residence until 31 December 2019. She then moved in with her partner in a house her partner owns, and let the flat to tenants. She never lived in the flat again. She sold it on 31 December 2025, making a gain (before any relief) of £140,000. For simplicity, treat each month as equal in length, and assume no relief other than private residence relief applies and that Kemi never shared occupation of the flat with any tenant.
What is Kemi's chargeable gain on the sale, before the annual exempt amount?

item.title: Interest on estate money held in client account during an administration (rule 7)
item.description:
Pemberton Hale LLP acts for the executors of the late Mrs Okafor. It has held £180,000 of estate money in its general client account for eight months while the house is sold and the estate administered. The firm's client care letter says nothing about interest. A partner suggests the firm should keep the interest earned on the money, because it is held in a pooled general client account rather than a separate deposit account.
Which of the following best describes the firm's obligation regarding interest?

item.title: Paying out more than is held for an estate client and replacing the shortfall (rules 5.3 and 6.1)
item.description:
Bryn & Adeyemi Solicitors acts for the executors of the late Mr Lindqvist. The client ledger for the estate shows £2,000 held in client account. At the fee earner's request, the cashier pays £3,500 from the general client account to settle an estate liability, because the fee earner expects £20,000 from the deceased's bank to arrive next week. The payment has been made. The firm's COFA discovers it the same day.
Which of the following best describes what the firm must now do?

item.title: Residual balance of £500 or less after an estate is distributed: payment to charity
item.description:
Seven years ago Garside Mehta LLP finished administering an estate and accounted to all the beneficiaries. A tax refund of £120 later arrived for one residuary beneficiary, Mr Ferreira, and was paid into client account. The firm has written to his last known addresses, emailed and telephoned him, and searched online, without success. The ledger still shows £120 held for him. The firm spent £60 on a tracing search.
Which of the following best describes what the firm may do with the £120?

item.title: Estate money in a joint account with a lay executor: which Accounts Rules apply (rules 9 and 12)
item.description:
Sterling Acheampong LLP acts for Raj, the sole executor of his late aunt's estate. With Raj's agreement, £60,000 of estate money is placed in a deposit account opened in the joint names of the firm and Raj. Both must sign any withdrawal. The firm also holds other client money in its general client account. The firm's cashier asks which requirements of the SRA Accounts Rules apply to the joint account.
Which of the following best describes the firm's obligations in relation to the joint account?

item.title: Deposit received as stakeholder on exchange is client money (rule 2.1(b))
item.description:
Hollis Nwosu LLP acts for Danuta on the sale of her house. Contracts are exchanged today. Under the contract, the buyer's solicitors send the 10% deposit of £45,000 to Hollis Nwosu LLP to hold 'as stakeholder' until completion. The firm's trainee asks how the money should be treated.
Which of the following best describes how the firm must treat the deposit?

item.title: Mixed payment from a buyer client covering completion money and a delivered bill (rule 4.2)
item.description:
Fenwick Rahman Solicitors acts for Jerome on his purchase of a flat. The firm has already delivered a bill of costs to Jerome for £1,200 including VAT, which is unpaid. Two days before completion Jerome sends a single bank transfer of £61,200 to the firm's general client account: £60,000 is the balance of the purchase money needed for completion, and £1,200 is to pay the bill.
Which of the following best describes how the firm should deal with the £61,200?

item.title: Accountant's report exemption: both the average and maximum balance limits must be met (rule 12.2)
item.description:
Calder Osei, a small residential conveyancing firm, has an accounting period running from 1 May 2025 to 30 April 2026. It holds client money and reconciles its client accounts monthly. The average of its twelve reconciliation balances is £8,400. The highest reconciliation balance, at the end of a month in which several completions were pending, is £265,000. No client money came from the Legal Aid Agency. The firm's COFA believes the firm does not need an accountant's report for the period.
Which of the following best describes the firm's obligation for that accounting period?

item.title: Status of Privy Council decisions in the courts of England and Wales (Willers v Joyce)
item.description:
In October 2026 a High Court judge in London is trying a common law claim in England and Wales. The defendant, Okonjo Ltd, relies on a 2018 decision of the Court of Appeal (Civil Division) which is directly in point. The claimant, Priya Raman, relies on a 2024 decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council on an appeal from an overseas jurisdiction whose common law on the point is the same as that of England and Wales. The Board said that the 2018 Court of Appeal decision was wrong, but it did not direct that courts in England and Wales should treat its own decision as representing English law. There is no relevant decision of the House of Lords or the Supreme Court.
Which of the following best describes how the High Court judge should proceed?

item.title: When an Act with no commencement provision comes into force (Interpretation Act 1978 s.4)
item.description:
The (fictional) Harbour Moorings Act 2026 is an Act of the UK Parliament. It received Royal Assent at 3.30 pm on Tuesday 10 March 2026. Section 5 of the Act imposes a new duty on mooring operators. Nothing in the Act, or in any other legislation, makes provision for when section 5 is to come into force. Kwame Mensah, a mooring operator in England, asks his solicitor when the duty in section 5 took effect.
When did section 5 come into force?

item.title: Using explanatory notes and Law Commission reports as aids to interpretation (R (O) v SSHD)
item.description:
In a 2026 claim in the High Court, the parties disagree about the meaning of a phrase in section 9 of a 2021 Act of Parliament. Counsel for the claimant, Femi Adebayo, wishes to rely on two documents: the Explanatory Notes published with the Act, and a Law Commission report which recommended the reform the Act was passed to make. Counsel for the defendant argues that neither document can be looked at unless the phrase is first shown to be ambiguous.
Which of the following best describes the use the court may make of these documents?

item.title: Purposive interpretation and developments Parliament did not foresee (Quintavalle)
item.description:
The (fictional) Inland Waters Safety Act 1999 provides that no person may operate a 'powered craft' on an inland lake in England without a safety licence. Section 1 defines a powered craft as 'a vessel driven by an engine, the vessel being treated as powered from the moment its fuel is ignited'. The Act was passed after a series of serious accidents to swimmers, and it sets up a detailed licensing regime. In 2026 Joaquim Silva is prosecuted for operating an unlicensed battery-electric hydrofoil board, a type of craft unknown in 1999, at high speed on a lake. He argues that no fuel is ever ignited in his craft, so it cannot be a powered craft.
Which of the following best describes how the court is likely to approach the interpretation of section 1?

item.title: Presumption of mens rea where a statutory offence is silent (B v DPP)
item.description:
The (fictional) Cash Couriers Act 2025 provides in section 2: 'A person who recruits a person under the age of 18 to carry cash for reward commits an offence', punishable by up to 10 years' imprisonment. The Act says nothing about the defendant's state of mind and contains no other relevant provision. Rhys Morgan is charged with recruiting Danny, aged 17. Rhys says he honestly believed that Danny was 19, although the prosecution argues that his belief was unreasonable because Danny looked young and was in school uniform.
Which of the following best describes the mental element the court is likely to require as to Danny's age?

item.title: Bilingual Acts of Senedd Cymru: equal status of the Welsh and English texts
item.description:
An Act of Senedd Cymru which received Royal Assent in 2023 was enacted in both Welsh and English. In a 2026 dispute in Cardiff about a planning duty under the Act, the solicitor for Gwen Prys notices that the Welsh text of one section appears to bear a narrower meaning than the English text, and the narrower meaning favours her client. The other side argues that the English text must prevail.
Which of the following best describes the status of the two texts?

item.title: Senedd Cymru legislative competence: provisions applying in relation to England (GoWA 2006 s.108A)
item.description:
An Act of Senedd Cymru passed in 2025 regulates bus services. Section 12 of the Act requires every local authority in England whose area borders Wales to publish a cross-border bus timetable each year. The provision is not ancillary to any other provision. Cheshire-based campaigner Amira Haddad asks a solicitor whether the English local authorities are legally bound by section 12.
Which of the following best describes the legal position?

item.title: Rights of audience: a litigant in person and a lay friend (Legal Services Act 2007)
item.description:
Darius Farahani is the claimant in a fast track claim in the County Court in England. He has no solicitor and is acting in person. At the trial he wants his friend Kemi, who is not a lawyer and holds no professional qualification, to stand up and make his closing submissions to the judge for him. Kemi will not be paid.
Which of the following best describes the rights of audience at the trial?

item.title: Ministers and judicial independence (Constitutional Reform Act 2005 s.3)
item.description:
A government minister, who is not the Lord Chancellor, is concerned about a pending High Court case in which a government department is the defendant. He asks his private office to arrange a private telephone call with the judge hearing the case, so that he can explain the government's concerns about the possible consequences of a ruling against the department. He does not intend to threaten the judge.
Which of the following best describes the minister's proposed conduct?

item.title: Constitutional statutes and implied repeal (Thoburn v Sunderland City Council)
item.description:
In 2026 a claimant argues in the High Court that a provision of a (fictional) 2025 Act of Parliament on local tax collection is inconsistent with a provision of the Human Rights Act 1998, and that the 2025 Act has therefore impliedly repealed the 1998 provision so far as the two conflict. The 2025 Act does not mention the Human Rights Act 1998, and its words are general. The claimant also points to a statement by the minister in Parliament suggesting that the Bill was intended to override 'any earlier legislation'.
Which of the following best describes how the court is likely to approach the implied repeal argument, applying Thoburn v Sunderland City Council?

item.title: Prerogative power and statute covering the same ground (De Keyser principle, Miller)
item.description:
After severe flooding in 2026, the (fictional) Flood Defence (Emergency Powers) Act 2024 gives the Secretary of State power to take temporary possession of private land for emergency flood defences, subject to paying compensation assessed under a statutory scheme. The Secretary of State takes possession of a field owned by Lowri Evans in England, but states that she is acting under the royal prerogative, so that only a discretionary ex gratia payment will be made.
Which of the following best describes the lawfulness of relying on the prerogative?

item.title: Legal status of the Sewel convention for Wales (GoWA 2006 s.107(6) and Miller)
item.description:
In 2026 the UK Parliament passes an Act changing the law on school admissions in Wales, a devolved matter. The Senedd voted to refuse its legislative consent to the Bill. The Welsh Government asks whether it can obtain a court ruling that the Act is invalid, or at least that Parliament acted unlawfully, because section 107(6) of the Government of Wales Act 2006 recognises that Parliament will not normally legislate on devolved matters without the Senedd's consent.
Which of the following best describes the legal position?

item.title: Parliamentary privilege and prosecution of MPs for false expenses claims (R v Chaytor)
item.description:
Gareth Oduya, a Member of Parliament, is charged with false accounting in the Crown Court. The prosecution alleges that he submitted dishonest claims for parliamentary expenses to the House of Commons authorities. He argues that the prosecution is barred by parliamentary privilege, relying on article 9 of the Bill of Rights 1689 (freedom of speech and debates or proceedings in Parliament ought not to be impeached or questioned in any court) and on the House's exclusive cognisance of its internal affairs.
Which of the following best describes whether the prosecution may proceed?

item.title: Advance notice of a public procession (Public Order Act 1986 s.11)
item.description:
Hana Kowalski is organising a march through the centre of Leeds on Saturday 21 November 2026 to publicise a campaign to save a local hospital. It is not a procession commonly or customarily held in the area, and it is not a funeral procession. It is reasonably practicable to give advance notice. She asks her solicitor what notice she must give.
Which of the following best describes the notice requirement?

item.title: Breach of the peace: definition and the power to prevent an imminent breach
item.description:
During a protest outside a factory in England, PC Marsh sees Lina Petrova, a protester, shouting at a counter-protester. She then raises her fist and moves towards him, and PC Marsh reasonably believes that she is about to strike him. PC Marsh takes hold of Lina and moves her away. Later Lina's solicitor is asked whether Lina can be prosecuted for 'the offence of breach of the peace' and whether PC Marsh was entitled to act before any blow was struck.
Which of the following best describes the legal position?

item.title: Refusing JR relief where the outcome would not be substantially different (SCA 1981 s.31(2A))
item.description:
Ashbury District Council decided to close a public library in England. Ines Carvalho, a regular user, brought a claim for judicial review, arguing that the council failed to carry out the consultation its own published policy required. At the substantive hearing the High Court accepts that the failure to consult was unlawful. However, on the evidence it concludes that it is highly likely that the outcome for Ines would not have been substantially different if the council had consulted properly. No reasons of exceptional public interest arise.
Which of the following best describes the court's position on relief?

item.title: Substantive legitimate expectation and whether detrimental reliance is required (Re Finucane)
item.description:
In January 2025 Brenton Borough Council wrote to each of the twelve traders who hold pitches in its covered market in England. The letter stated, without any qualification, that their pitches would not be relocated before January 2030. In 2026 the council resolves to relocate the traders to an outdoor site in order to let the hall for events, and it puts forward no overriding public interest beyond a modest increase in rental income. The traders cannot show that they spent money or changed their position because of the letter. They seek judicial review.
Which of the following best describes the traders' prospects of establishing a legitimate expectation claim?

item.title: Who may bring a Human Rights Act claim, and when (HRA 1998 s.7)
item.description:
In August 2025 officers of a local council in England entered and searched the home of Tomasz Nowak without lawful authority, which he says breached his right to respect for private and family life under Article 8. In October 2026, 14 months later, Tomasz wants to bring proceedings against the council under s.7(1)(a) of the Human Rights Act 1998. A national privacy charity, which was not itself affected by the search, also wants to bring its own claim against the council about the same search. No stricter time limit applies to the procedure to be used.
Which of the following best describes the position?

item.title: Effect of Strasbourg case law in domestic courts (HRA 1998 s.2)
item.description:
In a 2026 High Court claim about the right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights, counsel for the claimant, Nadia Chowdhury, relies on a recent Grand Chamber judgment of the European Court of Human Rights in a case against another Council of Europe state. Counsel tells the judge that, under the Human Rights Act 1998, the High Court is legally bound to follow that judgment.
Which of the following best describes the duty of the High Court in relation to the Strasbourg judgment?

item.title: Conflict between assimilated EU legislation and an Act of Parliament after 2023 (EUWA 2018 s.5)
item.description:
In 2026 a tribunal in England finds an irreconcilable conflict between a provision of a 2017 EU Regulation, which forms part of domestic law as assimilated direct legislation, and a provision of a 2015 Act of the UK Parliament. Before the end of 2023 the Regulation would have prevailed under the principle of the supremacy of EU law. Assume that no regulations have been made under s.7(1) of the Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023 for this provision, and that the Withdrawal Agreement is not relevant.
Which of the following best describes which provision prevails?

item.title: Police duty of care for positive acts during an arrest (Robinson v CC West Yorkshire)
item.description:
Two police officers in England decide to arrest a suspected drug dealer, Kyle, on a busy high street at lunchtime. They know he is likely to try to run. They approach him while Edna Price, aged 79, is walking immediately beside him. Kyle struggles, and he and both officers fall on top of Edna, breaking her hip. Edna sues the chief constable in negligence. The chief constable argues that the police owe no duty of care to members of the public when they are suppressing crime.
Which of the following best describes whether the officers owed Edna a duty of care?

item.title: The omissions principle: when a duty to prevent harm arises
item.description:
Your client wants to understand when English law (England and Wales) imposes a duty of care on a person to prevent harm to another that the person did not create. In each situation below, assume the harm was foreseeable, the person could easily have prevented it, and they did nothing.
In which of the following situations is a duty of care to prevent the harm most likely to arise?

item.title: Objective standard of care for a defendant with mental illness (Dunnage v Randall)
item.description:
Gareth suffers from paranoid schizophrenia. During a psychotic episode at his home in England he poured petrol around his kitchen and it ignited, seriously burning his cousin Leah, who was visiting and trying to calm him. The agreed psychiatric evidence is that Gareth's illness very substantially impaired his ability to control what he did, but that it did not completely destroy his voluntary control or his responsibility for his actions. A reasonable person would not have handled petrol in that way. Leah sues Gareth in negligence.
Which of the following best states whether Gareth is in breach of duty?

item.title: Professional standard and disclosure of material risks (Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board)
item.description:
Ines, a professional dancer, consults Mr Haddad, an orthopaedic surgeon in an NHS hospital in England, about knee surgery. She tells him that her career depends on full mobility in her legs. He recommends surgery but does not mention a 1% risk of permanent nerve damage causing foot drop, or the option of a longer course of physiotherapy instead. Expert evidence shows that a responsible body of orthopaedic surgeons would not mention a risk as low as 1%. Ines does not ask about risks. The nerve damage occurs and ends her career.
Which of the following best describes whether Mr Haddad breached his duty of care in failing to tell Ines about the risk?

item.title: Mesothelioma and multiple employers: joint and several liability (Compensation Act 2006 s.3)
item.description:
Terence worked as a lagger for three companies in England. Each negligently exposed him to asbestos: Allbright Ltd for 10 years, Brennan Ltd for 5 years and Castell Ltd for 5 years. He has now been diagnosed with mesothelioma. Because of the nature of the disease, it is impossible to say which exposure caused it. All three companies are still trading. Terence sues only Brennan Ltd, and it is accepted that Brennan Ltd is liable in tort because its exposure materially increased the risk of his illness.
Which of the following best describes Brennan Ltd's liability to Terence?

item.title: Pure economic loss caused by a negligent act: power cut damages calculation (Spartan Steel)
item.description:
Forgewell Ltd runs a glass-making plant in England around the clock. Contractors digging up a nearby road negligently cut the cable supplying electricity to the plant, and the power is off for 12 hours. A batch of glass in the furnace at the time is ruined, reducing its value by £1,200. Had that batch been completed, Forgewell would have made a profit of £900 on it. Forgewell also proves that it would have made a further profit of £4,500 on new batches it could not start while the power was off. The contractors admit negligence.
Applying the leading authority on economic loss caused by a negligent act, how much is Forgewell likely to recover from the contractors?

item.title: Negligent misstatement by a solicitor to the opposite party (Steel v NRAM)
item.description:
Hollins LLP, a firm of solicitors in England, acts for Dorrance Ltd, which is selling one of four commercial units mortgaged to Northgate Bank plc. Northgate is a commercial lender and is not using its own solicitor for the release. A partner at Hollins carelessly emails Northgate stating that Dorrance will repay its entire loan on completion and asking Northgate to release its charges over all four units. In fact, only part of the loan is to be repaid. Northgate does not check the email against its own loan records, which would have shown the error, and releases all its security. Dorrance later becomes insolvent and Northgate sues Hollins LLP in negligence for its loss.
Which of the following best describes whether Hollins LLP owed Northgate a duty of care in respect of the email?

item.title: Disclaimer of liability for negligent advice to a non-client business (UCTA 1977 ss.2(2), 11(3), 13)
item.description:
Vantage Surveyors LLP values a warehouse in England for Brightline Bank plc, which is considering a loan to Kestrel Logistics Ltd to buy it. Vantage knows that Kestrel will see the report and is likely to rely on it in deciding whether to buy. The report contains a prominent notice: 'No responsibility is accepted to any person other than Brightline Bank plc.' Kestrel, which is buying the warehouse for its business, relies on the report. The valuation was carelessly prepared and Kestrel suffers financial loss. There is no contract between Vantage and Kestrel.
Which of the following best describes the effect of the notice on any claim by Kestrel against Vantage in negligence?

item.title: Rescuers and primary victim status in psychiatric injury claims
item.description:
Amara, an off-duty nurse, is driving on a motorway in England when she comes upon a serious collision caused by the negligence of a lorry driver, Piotr. She stops and spends an hour helping injured strangers from their cars, some of whom die. Traffic has been stopped, and at no point was she in any physical danger or did she reasonably believe she was. She has no relationship with any of the victims. She later develops post-traumatic stress disorder and sues Piotr.
Which of the following best describes Amara's likely position?

item.title: Remoteness: foreseeability of the type of harm, not the precise manner (Jolley v Sutton LBC)
item.description:
A housing association in England owns the grassed common area of a block of flats where children regularly play. An abandoned caravan with broken windows has been left there for over a year, despite residents' complaints. The association accepts that it was negligent in failing to remove the caravan, because children might be cut by the broken glass. Two 13-year-old boys decide to turn the caravan into a den. They jack up one end to fix the wheels, and the caravan topples onto one of them, Tobias, breaking his pelvis. The association argues that the only foreseeable risk was of cuts from broken glass.
Which of the following best describes whether Tobias's injury is too remote?

item.title: What the estate can recover (Law Reform (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1934 s.1)
item.description:
Callum, aged 38, was seriously injured in England in a crash caused by the negligence of a delivery driver. He spent three weeks in hospital in great pain and then died of his injuries. Before the accident he earned £60,000 a year and expected to work until 67. His executor brings a claim for the benefit of his estate under the Law Reform (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1934.
Which of the following heads of loss is NOT recoverable in the estate's claim?

item.title: Who may claim bereavement damages under the Fatal Accidents Act 1976 s.1A
item.description:
Jade, aged 24, was killed in England when a negligently driven van hit her. She was not married and had no civil partner. For the 18 months before her death she lived with her boyfriend, Ravi, as a couple in a flat they rented together. Her parents, with whom she was very close, are both alive. Ravi and Jade's parents each want to claim the statutory bereavement award from the van driver's insurers.
Who is entitled to bereavement damages under the Fatal Accidents Act 1976?

item.title: Effect of contributory negligence on damages (Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945 s.1)
item.description:
Faisal was crossing a road in England while looking at his phone when he was hit by a car driven by Grace, who was speeding. Faisal suffered a broken leg. The court finds that Grace was negligent, but that Faisal was also at fault for not looking where he was going and that his fault contributed to his injury. His damages, ignoring his own fault, are assessed at £40,000.
Which of the following best describes the effect of Faisal's fault on his claim?

item.title: Volenti and passengers in motor vehicles (Road Traffic Act 1988 s.149)
item.description:
Mia accepted a lift home from a party in England from her friend Jonah, knowing that he had drunk a lot of alcohol. Before setting off, at Jonah's insistence, she signed a note saying: 'I travel entirely at my own risk and will not sue Jonah for any injury.' Jonah, whose use of the car was covered by compulsory motor insurance, drove negligently and crashed, injuring Mia. Jonah's insurers argue that Mia consented to the risk.
Which of the following best describes the insurers' argument?

item.title: Illegality: losses flowing from the claimant's own crime (Henderson v Dorset Healthcare)
item.description:
Rosalind has paranoid schizophrenia. Her mental health trust in England negligently failed to return her to hospital when her condition deteriorated, and she suffered several weeks of worsening psychotic symptoms. During a psychotic episode she killed her mother. She pleaded guilty to manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility, the court accepting that her responsibility was substantially reduced, and she was made subject to a hospital order. The trust admits negligence. Rosalind claims damages for: (1) the worsening psychotic symptoms before the killing; (2) her loss of liberty while detained under the hospital order; (3) depression and guilt caused by having killed her mother; and (4) the share of her mother's estate she lost because the court made an order under the Forfeiture Act 1982.
Which of these heads of loss is Rosalind likely to be able to recover?

item.title: Defective work equipment due to a third party (Employer's Liability (Defective Equipment) Act 1969)
item.description:
Oakridge Joinery Ltd buys a set of power saws from a reputable manufacturer and checks them on delivery, as a reasonable employer would. One saw has a hidden manufacturing defect which no reasonable inspection would have revealed. While using the saw in the course of his employment at Oakridge's workshop in England, Darius, an employee, is injured when the blade guard fails because of the defect. Oakridge argues that it was not at fault and that Darius should sue the manufacturer.
Which of the following best describes Oakridge's liability to Darius?

item.title: Vicarious liability stage one: independent contractors (Barclays Bank v Various Claimants)
item.description:
Harrow & Vale Logistics Ltd requires job applicants to pass a medical examination. It arranges for applicants to see Dr Fenwick, a self-employed GP who runs his own practice with many patients and corporate clients. The company books the appointments and sends him a form, and pays him a fee for each report. He chooses how to conduct the examinations, may refuse a booking, and carries his own professional insurance. During examinations at his own surgery in England, Dr Fenwick sexually assaults several applicants. They sue Harrow & Vale Logistics Ltd, alleging that it is vicariously liable.
Which of the following best describes whether the company is vicariously liable?

item.title: Vicarious liability stage two: close connection and an assault on a customer (Mohamud v WM Morrison)
item.description:
Kwame is employed by Fuelstop Ltd as a cashier at a petrol station kiosk in England. His job is to serve customers and deal with their questions. A customer, Mr Varga, asks politely whether he can print some documents. Kwame swears at him and orders him to leave. Mr Varga walks back to his car on the forecourt. Kwame follows him, opens the passenger door, tells him never to come back to 'my' petrol station and punches him repeatedly. Fuelstop Ltd had never authorised violence and had no reason to think Kwame was dangerous.
Which of the following best describes whether Fuelstop Ltd is vicariously liable for the assault?

item.title: Occupier's liability for a contractor's faulty work (Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 s.2(4)(b))
item.description:
Elmhurst Leisure Ltd runs a gym in England. It hires Liftline Services Ltd, a well-established, properly accredited lift engineering company with good references, to repair the passenger lift. After the work, Elmhurst obtains Liftline's test certificate confirming the lift is safe. Unknown to Elmhurst, a Liftline engineer carelessly fitted a faulty cable, and nothing would have revealed this to a non-specialist. A week later the lift drops suddenly, injuring Priya, a gym member.
Which of the following best describes Elmhurst's likely liability to Priya under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957?

item.title: Obvious risks and freely chosen dangerous activities (Tomlinson v Congleton BC)
item.description:
A local council in England runs a country park with a large lake. Signs at the entrance and by the water say 'Dangerous water. No swimming'. Many people ignore the signs. Ollie, aged 20, who has visited the park since childhood and knows the lake well, wades into water a little above his knees and plunges forward head first. He strikes the sandy bottom and suffers a serious spinal injury. The lake has no hidden hazards and is no more dangerous than any ordinary stretch of open water. Ollie argues that the council should have made the beaches inaccessible, which it had considered doing.
Which of the following best describes the council's likely liability to Ollie?

item.title: Excluding liability for personal injury to a consumer visitor (Consumer Rights Act 2015 s.65)
item.description:
Bounce Zone Ltd runs a trampoline park in England. Every customer pays for entry and must tick a box online confirming they have read a notice which says: 'Bounce Zone accepts no liability for any injury, however caused, including injury caused by our negligence.' The same notice is displayed at the entrance. Hannah, a customer, is injured when a trampoline collapses because Bounce Zone's staff negligently failed to replace a worn spring they had been told about.
Which of the following best describes the effect of the notice on Hannah's claim for her injury?

item.title: Who is liable for a defective product under the Consumer Protection Act 1987 s.2
item.description:
Hartwell Supermarkets plc sells electric kettles under its own brand, 'Hartwell Home', with no other maker's name on them. The kettles are made in Malaysia by Sunlit Appliances Sdn Bhd and imported into the United Kingdom by Corran Imports Ltd, which sells them to Hartwell in the course of its business. Zara buys one from a Hartwell store in England. A defect in the kettle causes it to split, and Zara is scalded. She wants to claim under Part I of the Consumer Protection Act 1987.
Which of the following best describes who is liable to Zara under Part I of the Act?

item.title: Who can sue in private nuisance: an interest in land is required (Hunter, confirmed in Fearn v Tate)
item.description:
Mrs Okafor owns the freehold of a house in England and lives there with her adult son, Samuel, who has no tenancy or other legal interest in the property and lives there with her permission. A recycling plant opens next door and, for several months, produces constant loud noise and strong smells that substantially interfere with the use and enjoyment of the house. Both Mrs Okafor and Samuel want to sue the plant operator in private nuisance.
Which of the following best describes who can sue in private nuisance?

item.title: Defences in private nuisance: coming to the nuisance and planning permission (Coventry v Lawrence)
item.description:
Six years ago, Thornfield Raceway Ltd began holding motocross events on its land in rural England, with planning permission for that use. Two years ago, Ms Adeyemi bought a farmhouse nearby and moved in, using it as her home, as previous owners had done. The noise from the events substantially interferes with the use and enjoyment of her home and, the court finds, amounts to a nuisance. Thornfield argues that (1) Ms Adeyemi came to the nuisance, knowing about the events when she bought, and (2) its activities have planning permission.
Which of the following best describes Thornfield's arguments?

item.title: Rylands v Fletcher: strict liability for property damage but not personal injury
item.description:
Fenbrook Chemicals Ltd stores large quantities of a highly corrosive industrial solvent in tanks on its site in England, an extraordinary use of land carrying an increased danger to neighbours if the solvent escapes. Despite Fenbrook having taken all reasonable care, a tank fails and the solvent escapes onto the neighbouring farm owned and occupied by Mr Lindqvist. It ruins crops and contaminates his land. Mr Lindqvist also suffers burns to his hands when trying to stop the flow. Damage of this kind from an escape was foreseeable.
Which of the following best describes Mr Lindqvist's claim under the rule in Rylands v Fletcher?

item.title: Certainty of subject matter: unallocated generic goods (Re Goldcorp)
item.description:
Sterling Vault Ltd, an online dealer in England, sold silver coins to members of the public on an 'unallocated' basis. Its terms said the coins were 'stored and insured on your behalf', but no coins were ever set aside or identified for any customer, and the company remained free to buy coins from any source to meet delivery requests. The company is now insolvent and its bank holds a valid floating charge over all its assets, which has crystallised. Its remaining stock of silver coins is far smaller than the total quantity customers paid for. The customers argue that the company holds its remaining coins on trust for them.
Which of the following best describes the customers' position in respect of the remaining coins?

item.title: Certainty of objects for a discretionary trust: the 'is or is not' test
item.description:
By a trust deed made in England in 2023, Rosalind Achebe transferred £900,000 to trustees directing that they 'shall each year distribute the income among such of the employees and former employees of Brightwater Logistics Ltd, and their spouses and dependants, as the trustees in their absolute discretion select'. The class is likely to exceed 4,000 people. The company's records of former employees are incomplete, so it is impossible to draw up a complete list of everyone in the class. The words used in the deed are clear in meaning. Rosalind has died and her executors argue that the trust is void.
Which of the following best describes the validity of the trust?

item.title: Oral declaration of trust of land: LPA 1925 s.53(1)(b)
item.description:
Owen Fairweather is the sole registered proprietor of a buy-to-let flat in Leeds, England. Over dinner he tells his adult sister Beatrix, 'From today I hold the flat on trust for you.' Nothing is put in writing. Beatrix has paid nothing towards the flat and has not changed her position in reliance on what Owen said. A year later Owen tells Beatrix he has changed his mind and intends to keep the flat.
Can Beatrix enforce the trust against Owen?

item.title: Oral direction to trustees to hold for another: s.53(1)(c) LPA 1925
item.description:
Kemal Arslan and Ruth Okafor hold 20,000 shares in a listed company on bare trust for Dalia Haddad absolutely. Dalia telephones the trustees and tells them that from now on they are to hold her interest in the shares on trust for her adult son, Idris. The trustees agree. Nothing is put in writing and the legal title to the shares stays with Kemal and Ruth. Dalia later dies. Her valid will leaves her whole estate to a cancer research charity.
Who is beneficially entitled to the shares?

item.title: Imperfect gift of shares not saved as a declaration of trust (Milroy v Lord)
item.description:
Geraldine Moss owned 500 shares in Arden Fabrics Ltd, a private company registered in England. She wrote and signed a letter to her godson, Felix Mensah, saying 'I give you my 500 shares in Arden Fabrics', and posted it to him. She never signed a stock transfer form, kept the share certificate in her desk, and continued to receive the dividends. She died six months later. Her will appoints her solicitor as executor and leaves her residuary estate, which includes the shares, to her brother. Felix argues that Geraldine held the shares on trust for him.
Which of the following best describes Felix's position?

item.title: The rule in Re Rose: donor has done everything in their power
item.description:
Tomasz Nowak owned 1,000 shares in Vistula Joinery Ltd, a private company registered in England. Intending an immediate gift, he signed a valid stock transfer form in favour of his niece, Ana Kowalczyk, and handed it with the share certificate to the company secretary for registration. The articles give the directors no power to refuse to register a transfer. Before the next board meeting at which the transfer would have been registered, Tomasz died suddenly. His will leaves his residuary estate to his son, Piotr. The company has not yet registered Ana.
Who is entitled in equity to the shares?

item.title: Imperfect gift perfected by appointment as executor (Strong v Bird)
item.description:
In 2022 Wilfred Abara, who lived in Bristol, England, told his close friend Marta Silva: 'My Steinway piano is yours now, it's a present.' He meant this as an immediate gift, but the piano stayed in his house because Marta had no room for it, and no deed of gift was made. Until his death in 2026 Wilfred regularly told visitors that the piano belonged to Marta, and he never suggested he had changed his mind. His valid will appoints Marta as his sole executor and leaves his residuary estate to his cousin, Desmond. Marta has obtained a grant of probate.
Who is entitled to the piano?

item.title: Gift to a trust where the donor is one of several trustees (Choithram v Pagarani)
item.description:
Helena Brandt executed a trust deed creating the Brandt Family Trust for her grandchildren, naming herself and her two adult sons, Lukas and Max, as the trustees. Immediately after signing, in front of all three, she said: 'I now give my investment portfolio to the Brandt Family Trust.' She intended this to take effect at once. The portfolio stayed registered in Helena's sole name, and she signed no transfer to the three trustees. She died a month later. Her next of kin, who take her estate on intestacy, argue that the gift is incomplete.
Which of the following best describes the status of the portfolio?

item.title: Charitable purposes: identifying a valid charitable trust (Charities Act 2011)
item.description:
Gordon Pryce, who lives in Hull, England, is preparing his will. He asks you which of several proposed gifts would take effect as a valid charitable trust. Assume each gift is otherwise properly drafted, takes effect in England and Wales, and that there is no other evidence about public benefit beyond what is stated.
Which proposed gift is most likely to be a valid charitable trust?

item.title: Automatic resulting trust where express trusts do not exhaust the beneficial interest
item.description:
In 2019 Lucas Varga transferred £200,000 to two trustees by a deed which directed them 'to pay the income to my partner Nadia for the rest of her life'. The deed said nothing about who was to take the capital after Nadia's death, and there is no evidence that Lucas intended to give up any remaining interest in the fund. Nadia has just died. Lucas is alive.
Who is beneficially entitled to the £200,000 capital?

item.title: Presumed resulting trust: purchase money provided by another
item.description:
Hamid Rahimi paid the whole £300,000 price of a buy-to-let flat in Manchester, England, which was registered in the sole name of his business associate, Sean Doyle, because Hamid was abroad on a long work posting when the purchase had to be completed. They are not related, are not in a personal relationship, and neither has ever lived in the flat. There is no written declaration of trust and no evidence either way about whether Hamid intended a gift. Sean now claims that the flat is his.
Which of the following best describes the beneficial ownership of the flat?

item.title: Family home in joint names: the starting point (Stack v Dowden; Jones v Kernott)
item.description:
Ifeoma and Callum, an unmarried couple, bought a house in Nottingham, England, as their family home in 2014. It was transferred into their joint names, and both are liable on the mortgage. The transfer contains no declaration of their beneficial interests. Ifeoma provided 70% of the deposit. For twelve years they pooled their earnings in a joint account from which all household bills and mortgage payments were made. They have now separated, and Ifeoma claims a 70% share.
What is the starting point for deciding how the beneficial interest in the house is shared?

item.title: Quantifying shares after a change of intention: the 'fair share' rule (Jones v Kernott)
item.description:
Sunita and Gareth bought a house in Swindon, England, in joint names in 2006 as their family home, with no declaration of trust. They separated in 2011, when Gareth moved out. From then on Sunita alone paid the mortgage, insurance and repairs, and brought up their children in the house. Gareth stopped contributing and used his savings to buy a flat of his own. The court finds that, after the separation, the couple came to intend that their shares in the house would no longer be equal. However, there is no evidence, direct or by inference, of what proportions they intended.
How should the court decide the parties' beneficial shares?

item.title: Family home in one party's sole name: is there any beneficial interest at all?
item.description:
Rhys bought a house in Bristol, England, in his sole name in 2015, funding it with his savings and a mortgage in his sole name. His partner, Amara, moved in with him in 2017. Since then she has paid for some groceries and the occasional utility bill, but she contributed nothing to the purchase price or the mortgage. They never discussed who owned the house. They have now separated and Amara claims a half share. There is no written declaration of trust.
Which of the following best describes how the court will approach Amara's claim?

item.title: Requirements of proprietary estoppel: assurance, reliance and detriment
item.description:
Over fifteen years Bryn Hughes, who farmed in Herefordshire, England, repeatedly told his nephew Owain, 'Stick with me and this farm will be yours when I'm gone.' Relying on this, Owain worked full time on the farm for well below the going wage and turned down two better-paid jobs elsewhere. Nothing was ever put in writing and there was no contract. Shortly before he died, Bryn made a new will leaving the farm to a neighbour. Owain consults you.
Which of the following best describes Owain's position?

item.title: Who can be a trustee: appointment of a minor is void (LPA 1925 s.20)
item.description:
By her will, Precious Ndlovu, who died in England in 2025, left her investment portfolio to 'my brother Tendai and my daughter Rudo as trustees' on trust for her grandchildren. When Precious died, Tendai was 45 and Rudo was 16. Tendai asks what effect Rudo's age has on the trust.
Which of the following best describes the position?

item.title: Trustees' duties when investing: standard investment criteria and proper advice (TA 2000)
item.description:
Femi Adeyemi and Gwen Price are unpaid lay trustees of a £600,000 family trust in England. The trust deed contains no investment clause and does not exclude any statutory duty. They plan to invest the whole fund in the shares of a single technology company that was recommended in a friend's investment newsletter. They do not intend to take any advice, because they consider the opportunity too good to miss.
Which of the following best describes the trustees' duties?

item.title: Statutory maintenance: contingent beneficiary entitled to income at 18 (TA 1925 s.31)
item.description:
Harriet Quaye died in 2020. Her will left her residuary estate on trust for her grandson Zane 'if he attains the age of 25'. No one has a prior interest. The gift carries the intermediate income, and the will does not exclude or vary section 31 of the Trustee Act 1925. While Zane was a minor the trustees used part of the income for his school fees and accumulated the rest. Zane has just turned 18.
What is the trustees' position regarding the income of the trust fund from now on?

item.title: Self-dealing rule: trustee buying trust property
item.description:
Mairead Flynn and Colin Tate are the trustees of a will trust in England. The trust owns a holiday cottage in Cornwall. Mairead wants to buy the cottage herself. The trustees obtain an independent valuation, and Colin agrees to sell the cottage to Mairead at the full valuation figure. The will contains no clause authorising a trustee to buy trust property, the beneficiaries are not told, and the court's approval is not sought. A year later one of the adult beneficiaries learns of the sale and objects.
Which of the following best describes the validity of the sale?

item.title: Secret commission received by a trustee is held on trust (FHR European Ventures v Cedar)
item.description:
Oskar Lind, a trustee of a family trust in England, placed £400,000 of trust money with an investment manager. Without telling his co-trustees or the beneficiaries, he accepted a £15,000 'introduction commission' from the manager. He used the £15,000 to buy shares in his own name, which are now worth £25,000. The trust investment itself has performed well and the trust has suffered no loss. Oskar is now insolvent.
Which of the following best describes the beneficiaries' rights in respect of the commission?

item.title: Relief from liability for breach of trust: Trustee Act 1925 s.61
item.description:
Agnes Kirby, an unpaid lay trustee of a small family trust in England, distributed £30,000 to a beneficiary in reliance on written advice from the trust's solicitors that the beneficiary was entitled. The advice was wrong and the payment was a breach of trust. Agnes acted in good faith, followed the advice carefully, and had no reason to doubt it. The trust deed contains no exemption clause. The other beneficiaries now sue her.
On what basis may the court relieve Agnes from personal liability?

item.title: Limitation for breach of trust: future interests and s.21(3) Limitation Act 1980
item.description:
A trust in England gives Pearl a life interest, with remainder to Quentin absolutely. In March 2017 the trustee, Rupert, honestly but negligently made an unauthorised investment, which lost much of its value. The loss was reported to both beneficiaries in June 2018. Rupert did not keep or receive any of the trust money himself, there was no fraud, and nothing was concealed. Pearl died in January 2025. In March 2026 Quentin issued proceedings against Rupert for the loss to the capital.
Is Quentin's claim time-barred?

item.title: Tracing into a mixed bank account: the lowest intermediate balance rule
item.description:
Victor Mensah, a trustee, had £5,000 of his own money in his personal bank account. In breach of trust he paid in £20,000 of trust money, making a balance of £25,000. He then spent £22,000 from the account on a holiday and living expenses, leaving £3,000. A month later he paid £10,000 of his own salary into the account, bringing the balance to £13,000. He did not intend the salary payment to replace the trust money. Victor is now bankrupt and the beneficiaries wish to make a proprietary claim to the money in the account.
What is the maximum amount the beneficiaries can claim from the account by tracing?

item.title: Dishonest assistance: the trustee's honesty is irrelevant (Royal Brunei Airlines v Tan)
item.description:
Celia Osei, a trustee, honestly but wrongly believed that the trust deed allowed her to lend £150,000 of trust money to a property developer. She asked her accountant, Darius Webb, to arrange the transfer. Darius knew the loan was plainly outside the trustee's powers and knew that Celia mistakenly thought otherwise, but he said nothing and arranged the transfer. He received none of the trust money. The developer became insolvent and the money was lost. The beneficiaries sue Darius.
Which of the following best describes Darius's liability?

item.title: Knowing receipt: no liability for a bona fide purchaser who later learns of the breach
item.description:
In breach of trust, Lionel Grant, the sole trustee of a family trust in England, sold 5,000 trust shares to Imogen Clarke for their full market value. Imogen acted in good faith and had no notice, actual or constructive, that the sale was a breach of trust. Eighteen months later a beneficiary tells Imogen about the breach. She still holds the shares. The beneficiaries claim that she is now personally liable in knowing receipt.
Is Imogen liable in knowing receipt?

item.title: Acknowledging an earlier signature to two witnesses present together (Wills Act 1837 s.9)
item.description:
Delroy, an adult domiciled in England, wrote out and signed his will alone at his kitchen table one evening. The next morning he asked two neighbours, Agnieszka and Farid, to come in together. With both of them in the room at the same time, he pointed to his signature and said, 'That is my signature on my will.' Agnieszka then signed as a witness in Delroy's presence and went home; Farid signed in Delroy's presence ten minutes later, after Agnieszka had left. The will has no attestation clause. Delroy has now died.
Which of the following best describes whether the will was validly executed?

item.title: Testamentary capacity: Banks v Goodfellow, not the Mental Capacity Act 2005, as the test applied
item.description:
Winifred, aged 88, made a will in 2025 leaving her whole estate to her carer, Precious, and nothing to her son, Lewis. Eight months earlier she had been diagnosed with mild dementia. She has now died, domiciled in England. Lewis has entered a caveat and intends to challenge the will on the ground that Winifred lacked testamentary capacity. He asks you which legal test the court will apply to decide that question.
Which of the following best describes the test the court will apply?

item.title: Unattested alteration to a will made after execution (Wills Act 1837 s.21)
item.description:
Harriet's validly executed will, signed and witnessed in 2022, contains the clause 'I give £5,000 to my nephew Callum'. In 2024 Harriet drew a single line through '£5,000', leaving the figure clearly legible, and wrote '£15,000' above it. She initialled the change and dated it, but no one witnessed it and she did not re-execute the will or make a codicil. It is accepted that the change was made after the will was executed. Harriet has now died, domiciled in England.
Which of the following best describes Callum's entitlement?

item.title: Revocation by destruction must be by the testator or in their presence (Wills Act 1837 s.20)
item.description:
Rukhsana was in hospital when she telephoned her daughter, Zainab, and told her to go to Rukhsana's flat, find her will in the bureau and tear it up, because she no longer wanted it to take effect. Zainab did so that afternoon while Rukhsana remained in hospital. Rukhsana died a week later, domiciled in England, without making a new will. Her solicitors hold a copy of the will.
Which of the following best describes the status of Rukhsana's will?

item.title: Effect of divorce on gifts to, and appointment of, a former spouse (Wills Act 1837 s.18A)
item.description:
In 2018 Kwame made a will appointing his wife, Esi, as sole executrix and leaving his whole estate 'to my wife Esi, but if she dies before me, to such of my children as survive me in equal shares'. The will contains no other relevant provisions. Kwame and Esi divorced in England and the final order was made in 2025. Kwame died in 2026 without changing his will, survived by Esi and by their two adult children.
Which of the following best describes the effect of the divorce on Kwame's will?

item.title: Ademption of a specific gift of shares sold before death
item.description:
Marisol's will, made in 2020, leaves 'my 2,000 shares in Larkspur plc to my niece Inés' and the residue of her estate to a registered charity. In 2024 Marisol sold all her Larkspur plc shares and paid the proceeds into her savings account, where they remain identifiable. She did not acquire any further shares in Larkspur plc and owned none at her death in 2026. She died domiciled in England without changing her will.
Which of the following best describes Inés's entitlement?

item.title: Order of application of assets to debts and abatement of pecuniary legacies (AEA 1925 Sch.1 Pt II)
item.description:
Ngozi died in 2026, domiciled in England, leaving a valid will which gives: (1) 'my car' to her friend Asha; (2) £30,000 to her brother Ben; (3) £10,000 to her cousin Chloe; and (4) the residue of her estate to her neighbour Dev. The will says nothing about how debts are to be paid. Her estate consists of the car, worth £10,000, and money in the bank of £40,000. Her funeral, testamentary and administration expenses and debts total £20,000. The estate is solvent. Ignore inheritance tax.
Which of the following best describes how the estate will be distributed?

item.title: Lapse of a share of residue given to named beneficiaries in equal shares
item.description:
Thomas, who was unmarried and had no children, made a valid will leaving his residuary estate 'to my friends Olumide Adeyemi and Ravi Kapoor in equal shares'. The will contains no substitutional gift or survivorship clause. Ravi died in 2025 leaving two children. Thomas died in 2026, domiciled in England, survived by Olumide and by his own sister, Bronwen. Thomas's parents had both died before him.
Which of the following best describes who is entitled to Thomas's residuary estate?

item.title: Calculating children's shares on intestacy with a surviving spouse (statutory legacy £322,000)
item.description:
Pradeep died intestate on 3 June 2026, domiciled in England. He was survived by his wife, Kavita, and their two adult children, Arun and Leela. After payment of debts and expenses, his estate consists of personal chattels worth £30,000, a house in his sole name worth £520,000 and savings of £152,000. Assume the statutory legacy (fixed net sum) for a death on that date is £322,000. Ignore interest on the statutory legacy and inheritance tax.
How much will each child be entitled to under the intestacy rules?

item.title: Intestacy with no spouse, issue or parent: whole-blood sibling's issue before half-blood sibling
item.description:
Gethin died intestate in 2026, domiciled in England. He never married or formed a civil partnership and had no children. Both his parents died before him. His only full brother, Rhodri, died in 2023 leaving two adult children, Siân and Owain, who survived Gethin. Gethin was also survived by his half-sister, Mererid (they shared the same mother), and by his paternal grandmother, Gwen.
Which of the following best describes who is entitled to Gethin's estate?

item.title: Time limit for an Inheritance Act 1975 claim: six months from the grant
item.description:
Felicity's father died in January 2026, domiciled in England, leaving his whole estate to a charity. A grant of probate was issued to his executors seven months ago. Felicity, his adult daughter, now consults you about making a claim for reasonable financial provision from his estate. No distribution has yet been made.
Which of the following best describes the time limit position for Felicity's claim?

item.title: Cohabitant of less than two years: claiming under the 1975 Act as a person being maintained
item.description:
Mateus and Lorraine lived together in Mateus's house as if they were a married couple for 18 months until Mateus died suddenly in 2026, domiciled in England. They never married. Throughout that time Mateus paid the mortgage and all household bills, and Lorraine, who works part time on a low income, paid nothing towards them under any commercial arrangement. Mateus's will, made before they met, leaves everything to his brother. Lorraine asks whether she can bring a claim under the Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975.
Which of the following best describes Lorraine's position?

item.title: Priority for a grant where the sole executor predeceased (NCPR 1987 r.20)
item.description:
Beatrix's will appoints her brother, Lionel, as sole executor. It leaves £10,000 to her friend Saoirse and the residue of her estate to her two adult nieces, Amara and Josie, absolutely in equal shares. Lionel died two years before Beatrix. The will contains no other appointment of executors. Beatrix has now died, domiciled in England. Saoirse, Amara and Josie are all willing to act, and so is Lionel's own executor.
Which of the following best describes who has priority to take a grant and what type of grant will issue?

item.title: Minority interest on intestacy: two administrators required (Senior Courts Act 1981 s.114(2))
item.description:
Hamza died intestate in 2026, domiciled in England, leaving his wife, Nadia, and their son, Idris, aged 9. After debts, the estate (excluding personal chattels) is worth £600,000, which exceeds the statutory legacy. Nadia wishes to apply for the grant of letters of administration on her own, and no one else in the family is keen to be involved.
Which of the following best describes the position on the grant?

item.title: Executor who may wish to act later: power reserved rather than renunciation (NCPR 1987 rr.27 and 37)
item.description:
Vivienne's will appoints her two children, Oluwaseun and Hana, as executors. Vivienne has died, domiciled in England. Oluwaseun wants to apply for probate now. Hana is working overseas for the next year and does not want to be involved at present, but she says she may want to act as executor when she returns.
Which of the following is the most appropriate course?

item.title: Protecting personal representatives against unknown claims: s.27 Trustee Act 1925 notices
item.description:
Malik and Joanna are the executors of their late uncle, who ran a small antiques business from home before he died, domiciled in England. They have paid all the debts they know about and want to distribute the estate to the beneficiaries, but they are worried that there may be creditors of the business they do not know about.
Which of the following best describes the step they can take to protect themselves before distributing?

item.title: Property passing outside the will: joint tenancy survivorship and tenancy in common
item.description:
Kofi died in 2026, domiciled in England. His valid will leaves 'all my estate' to his daughter, Ama. At his death he owned: (1) his home, held with his partner, Efua, as beneficial joint tenants; (2) a buy-to-let flat, held with his brother, Yaw, as tenants in common in equal shares; and (3) a bank account in his sole name. No notice of severance was ever given in relation to the home.
Which of the following best describes what passes to Ama under Kofi's will?

item.title: Inheritance tax on death: nil-rate band, residence nil-rate band and charity exemption
item.description:
Seamus, a widower, died in July 2026, domiciled in England. He made no lifetime gifts, and no unused nil-rate band or residence nil-rate band is available to transfer from his late wife. His estate is worth £1,000,000, including his home, worth £400,000. By his will he leaves £50,000 to a registered charity, his home to his daughter, Niamh, and the residue (£550,000) to his nephew, Declan. Assume a nil-rate band of £325,000, a maximum residence nil-rate band of £175,000, a death rate of 40%, and that the estate does not qualify for the reduced rate for charitable giving. There are no debts and no other reliefs.
How much inheritance tax is payable on Seamus's death estate?

item.title: Failed potentially exempt transfer: tax with taper relief (IHTA 1984 s.7(4))
item.description:
On 1 March 2022 Babatunde gave £525,000 in cash to his son, Femi. He made no other lifetime gifts. Babatunde died on 1 September 2026, domiciled in England. Assume a nil-rate band of £325,000 both at the date of the gift and at death, a death rate of 40%, and ignore the annual exemption and all other exemptions and reliefs.
How much inheritance tax is payable on the gift to Femi as a result of Babatunde's death?

item.title: Business property relief unavailable for shares in an investment (property letting) company
item.description:
Lucinda died in 2026, domiciled in England, leaving all her shares in Lucinda Lettings Ltd to her son. She had owned all the issued shares for twelve years. The company is unquoted and its business consists entirely of owning and letting twelve residential flats on assured shorthold tenancies. Lucinda was a director and worked in the business full time.
Which of the following best describes the availability of business property relief (BPR) on the shares?

item.title: Occupiers' liability to skilled visitors and risks incident to their calling
item.description:
Dana owns and runs a café. A wall socket behind the counter has started sparking, so she calls out Kofi, a qualified electrician, and tells him exactly what the fault is. Kofi decides to work on the socket without isolating the electricity supply, to save time. He receives an electric shock and is injured. There is nothing else wrong with the premises.
Which of the following best describes Dana's likely liability to Kofi under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957?

item.title: Counter-offers and the rejection of an original offer
item.description:
On Monday Rhys emails Ola offering to sell her his vintage campervan for £18,000, adding: 'This offer is open until Friday.' On Wednesday Ola replies: 'I will pay £16,500 for it.' Rhys replies the same day: 'No, sorry.' On Thursday Ola emails: 'Fine, I accept your offer at £18,000.' Rhys has meanwhile decided to keep the campervan and refuses to sell.
Which of the following best describes the legal position?

item.title: Time limit for serving a claim form within the jurisdiction (CPR 7.5)
item.description:
A solicitor acts for a claimant in a contract claim against a supplier based in Leeds. The court issued the claim form on 10 February 2026. The solicitor intends to serve the claim form on the defendant at its registered office by first class post.
Which of the following correctly states the latest point by which the claimant must act to serve the claim form in time?

item.title: Removing a company director: ordinary resolution and special notice
item.description:
Maya holds 60% of the shares in Fernhill Joinery Ltd, a private company limited by shares that has adopted the model articles without amendment. She wants to remove Tom, one of the company's three directors. Tom has a written service contract with the company that still has two years to run. Maya would prefer to avoid a meeting and asks whether she can simply circulate a written resolution to the shareholders.
Which of the following best describes how Tom can be removed as a director?
